core_content.body_markdown:
## Co-location: what it gives you
Worth stating first, because the challenges are all consequences of losing it. Where teams share a place, you get one room where the plans and the progress are up on the wall, and relationships that grow close through proximity.

A dispersed team is one split across places, and often across time zones too. Virtual and remote are the other names for it. The technology has made this both more common and less painful, and home working rose in many organisations after the COVID-19 pandemic.

## Hybrid teams: the rule to hold
A specific instruction, and one worth holding: run it as a dispersed team even if most of the people happen to sit together. Doing so hands the same access and the same opportunities to everyone, as nearly as that can be managed.

Running the meeting in the room and dialling the remote people in creates two classes of membership. Treating everyone as remote levels it.

## Virtual teams: the seven challenges
| Challenge | What is lost |
|---|---|
| Trust and relationships | Depth and trust are harder to build through a screen than face to face |
| Communication | Degrades, taking understanding and empathy down with it |
| Spotting and resolving conflict | Harder to see conflict developing, and harder to resolve it |
| Less positive conflict | The result is less constructive challenge, the LO11 failure state arriving by default rather than by culture |
| Informal conversation | The unplanned talk that happens around a kettle or a corridor disappears, and with it goes some connection and sense of shared responsibility |
| Development, productivity and wellbeing | Personal and professional development and productivity can suffer; being isolated and lonely through the working day harms wellbeing, and those problems are much harder to notice and address at a distance |
| Diversity and practicalities | Differences in culture and language, generational differences, and the practical problem of different time zones |

The fourth row is not obvious: distance does not only reduce communication, it specifically reduces the *productive disagreement* a team needs. Silence on a call reads as consent far more easily than silence in a room.

The response APM gives: hearing out every individual, and understanding how they see it, matters more here than it would in a room.

## Virtual leadership: why the approach must differ
Tools enable this; they do not deliver it. Virtual leadership is built from the middle outward, and what sits in the middle is leadership style and a virtual mindset:

| Layer | What it requires |
|---|---|
| 1. Style and mindset | Facilitating rather than directing when working with remote colleagues and stakeholders. Knowing what people prefer and what they can do, and how trust gets built and kept |
| 2. Team norms | Agreement on how the team will communicate, collaborate and challenge, reached with everyone's preferences in the room |
| 3. Technology | Only then can technology implement team processes |

A leader who starts with tool selection has begun at layer three and skipped the two that decide whether it works.

A facilitative approach specifically, which connects to LO10's facilitation content. Remaining neutral, drawing out contributions, ensuring everyone can contribute and be heard. Those skills are optional in a room where people interrupt naturally; they are load-bearing on a call.

## Technology: what it has to be evaluated for
| Area | What it must support |
|---|---|
| Virtual meetings | Talking, facilitating, sharing information, reaching consensus, capturing notes |
| Workload management | Identifying tasks, allocating them, tracking them |
| Collaboration | Working on things together, holding a dialogue, getting at documents |

A social element, a clear process and a facilitative approach all improve a virtual meeting. The social element is deliberate, not decoration. It is the replacement for the informal conversation that distance removed.

## Leading dispersed teams: the organising principle
APM states it plainly: much of leading a dispersed team consists of rebuilding, by other means, whatever people would have got for free from sharing a room.

Everything else follows from that. Trust that would have formed naturally has to be built deliberately. Challenge that would have happened over a desk has to be invited explicitly. Distress that would have been visible has to be asked about.

key_definitions.plain_english: A handful of people pointed at one goal. On a project, assembled for the job and dissolved afterwards.
key_definitions.apm_definition: A small number of people working together towards a shared goal. In project-based working, teams are temporary and formed for a specific purpose.

key_definitions.plain_english: Turning the people you were given into a team. Rarely does a ready-made one arrive.
key_definitions.apm_definition: Transforming a group into an effective team, respecting team members as individuals with their own capabilities, preferences, cultural norms and expectations, and creating a positive working culture that enables high performance.

key_definitions.plain_english: People working on the same thing from different places. Increasingly the default rather than the exception.
key_definitions.apm_definition: A team separated by geography and possibly time zones. Also called a virtual or remote team.

key_definitions.plain_english: Getting out of the way and clearing the path. What good leadership looks like once a team can run itself.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The more subtle leadership role appropriate once a team is performing well, providing the team with the resources it needs to continue performing.

key_definitions.plain_english: The stage most projects forget. The team ends; the people carry on somewhere else, and that transition needs managing.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The final stage of team development, in which team members are helped to transition into their next roles.

key_definitions.plain_english: Some roles need deep expertise; some mostly need the method. Moving people through the second kind builds cover and broadens understanding.
key_definitions.apm_definition: A distinction used to provide role variety and build team resilience. Process roles carry little technical content and can be trained relatively easily, allowing team members to take on unfamiliar work.

key_definitions.plain_english: Leading remotely is not leading in a room with the video on. It starts with a different posture, not a different tool.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The starting point of virtual leadership development, alongside leadership style: a facilitative approach to working with remote colleagues and stakeholders, understanding preferences and skills, and how to build and maintain trust.

key_definitions.plain_english: The rules the team writes for itself about how it will work. Explicit for dispersed teams, because nothing gets absorbed by osmosis.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The agreed conventions for communication, collaboration and challenge, which must take everyone's preferences into account.

core_content.body_markdown:
## Diversity: what it means here
Diversity is about spanning the widest possible range of people. The dimensions APM names:

- ethnicity and race
- social class
- age
- gender, and gender identity
- sexual orientation
- the languages people speak
- mental health
- faith or religion
- ability, both physical and mental
- neurodivergence

Note how wide that is. Class, language and neurodivergence all appear, and none of them is a legally protected characteristic in the UK. Diversity as a concept is broader than the law's list.

## Diversity terms: five to keep separate
APM uses five terms, and they are not interchangeable.

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Diversity | Having the broadest range of different people |
| Inclusion | Creating an environment where everyone feels welcome |
| Belonging | Everyone feeling the environment is *theirs*, not somewhere they were let into |
| Advocacy | Using your voice on behalf of a group being marginalised or discriminated against |
| Allyship | Backing people from marginalised groups |

The progression from diversity → inclusion → belonging is the one to hold. Each is a step further, and each is harder.

## Protected characteristics: the ones the syllabus names
The syllabus lists characteristics which may cause a person to be treated less favourably:

| Characteristic |
|---|
| Age |
| Disability |
| Marriage and civil partnership |
| Pregnancy and maternity |
| Race |
| Religion or belief |
| Sex |
| Sexual orientation |

These are protected characteristics under the Equality Act 2010, which is where the framing comes from, not from the Body of Knowledge.

Two things worth knowing precisely:

1. The Act protects nine characteristics; the syllabus list names eight. The one not listed is gender reassignment. The syllabus says 'such as', so the list is illustrative rather than complete.
2. This is the legal floor, not the goal. Plenty of countries make discrimination unlawful, and the expectation on a project professional runs past that, into owning inclusion and belonging. Compliance with the Act stops you being unlawful. It does not produce a team where people can contribute.

## The legal frame: why it is not enough on its own
APM's position is that teams are stronger for their differences, and that they do best where people are valued for their capabilities instead of being run down for their weak spots.

That is a performance argument rather than a compliance one, and it is the stronger of the two. LO14b and 14c both build on it.

## Jurisdiction: why location matters
Worth carrying, because scenarios can be set anywhere: some jurisdictions require diversity, inclusion and cultural-difference training by law, and in many places certain expressions of conscious bias are themselves unlawful, putting both the individual and the organisation at risk of prosecution.

APM's own instruction where that arises: if unsure, project professionals should always seek advice.
core_content.outcome_title: What diversity covers, and the characteristics that attract less favourable treatment

core_content.body_markdown:
## Diversity benefits: the mechanism
The benefits of diversity are proven. The mechanism behind them is one fact: people genuinely perceive the world differently, and read the same situation through unlike filters. The result is a different angle on every part of a project, programme or portfolio.

Everything else follows from that single fact.

## Diversity benefits: what they are
| Benefit | How it arises |
|---|---|
| More perspectives | Different backgrounds and cultures bring different experiences to bear on the same problem |
| Broader skills | Irrelevant-seeming capabilities find useful applications in project work, making the team more adaptable |
| More effective problem-solving | More approaches available to any given problem |
| Greater creative thinking and innovation | Different perspectives produce ideas a uniform team would not reach |
| More robust decision-making | Options get tested from more angles before being chosen |
| Deeper empathy with end users | The more a team resembles the community it is building for, the better it designs and delivers something those users actually need |
| Strong community | An inclusive environment produces a stronger sense of community within the team |
| Greater adaptability and resilience | A broader range of personalities, experiences and skills lets a team tolerate and support one another and thrive under stress, and absorb a shock through fresh thinking, moving fast, and backing each other |

## 'From team members to customers': why the phrase matters
The syllabus phrase matters. Diversity is not only an internal staffing question: the deeper empathy with end users benefit is about the *output*, not the working environment.

A team that resembles the people it is building for understands them better. A team that does not will make confident assumptions about users it has never met, and those assumptions end up in the product. That is a delivery risk, not only an ethical one.

## Diversity plus inclusion: the equation behind it all
APM is unusually direct here, and this is the highest-value point in 14b:

| Combination | Result |
|---|---|
| Diversity without inclusion | Leaders cannot get the best from people. The perspectives are present but cannot be heard |
| Inclusion without diversity | Comfortable, short on new ideas, short on challenge, and poorly attuned to the society the project exists to serve |
| Diversity with inclusion | Enhanced team performance and better results |

A warm, welcoming, entirely homogeneous team is not the safe option. It is the groupthink condition from LO11 with better manners.

## Project professionals: why they can make a difference
A point some people dismiss: it is easy to assume a project manager has no real purchase on organisational culture. APM rejects that.

A project team gets built with a culture of its own, which puts its wellbeing in the project professional's hands. Assembling a diverse team is frequently a choice available to them, along with enough control to make that team an inclusive one.

A temporary team is built from scratch. That is an opportunity a line manager inheriting a permanent department does not get.

## Inclusive environments: how to build one
Start at the entry point. Inclusion starts with ensuring there are no barriers to entry, which probably means measuring who applies, who gets appointed, and who stays, particularly from underrepresented groups. Retention as well as appointment: hiring people into an environment they then leave is not inclusion.

At hiring:

- capability-based requirements set for each role
- open recruitment wherever possible
- blinded CVs where possible, with names, genders, ages and other personal identifiers removed before review
- a deliberate call on whether you are recruiting the strongest individuals or assembling the strongest team, with perspectives balanced across it

That last one is a genuine judgement call: the strongest individuals do not automatically compose the strongest team.

Once the team exists:

| Action | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Training in diversity, inclusion and cultural differences | Mandatory in some jurisdictions, good practice everywhere |
| Periodic surveys | Feedback on how the team actually feels, rather than how you assume they feel |
| Meeting structure and facilitation | So everyone can contribute and people listen |
| Echo and attribute | Where a contribution is not acknowledged, repeat the point and attribute it to the speaker |
| Recognition and celebration | Give recognition for collaboration and celebrate wins together |
| Mentoring and sponsorship | Gives people a route through the culture and someone to raise difficulties with. Not everyone finds it easy to promote themselves, and a sponsor can make sure their achievements get aired |
| Advocacy | Speaking up for someone being denied due respect, though it can strip power from the person even when kindly meant |
| Allyship | Supporting people without speaking for them, helping them secure a platform to speak for themselves. Check first that support is wanted, and what form it should take |
| Speak out | If you see prejudice, discrimination or disrespect, say so |

The advocacy-versus-allyship distinction is the one to hold from that table: advocacy speaks *for* someone, allyship helps them speak. APM flags that advocacy can disempower, which is why allyship is usually the better default.

And on leadership: the job is to set the standard and call out breaches of it. Everyone needs a line they will hold, and the willingness to challenge whoever steps over it.
core_content.outcome_title: Why diversity across the project creates a positive environment and innovative solutions

core_content.body_markdown:
## Bias: where it comes from
Human beings are most at ease around people who resemble them. That is the root, and stating it matters: bias is not presented as a moral failing found in bad people, but as a default human tendency that everyone has to work against.

It leads to discrimination, whose sources are prejudice and bias:

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| Discrimination | One person treated more or less favourably than another |
| Prejudice | Reaching a view before the relevant facts are in, usually off stereotypes or perceptions that have dated |
| Bias | Favouring or disfavouring someone, or their ideas, on something other than the merits |

Fairness, respect and wellbeing all suffer from either one.

## Conscious vs unconscious bias: the difference
| | Conscious (explicit) bias | Unconscious (implicit) bias |
|---|---|---|
| Awareness | People are aware of it and express it deliberately | Operates below conscious awareness, so people do not know it is happening |
| Roots | Upbringing, social conditioning, experiences, cultural norms | Beliefs, stereotypes and assumptions |
| How it shows | People or groups discriminated against, excluded or harassed because of who they are | Affects selection, recognition, working relationships and decision-making |
| Legal exposure | In many jurisdictions some expressions are illegal, exposing individuals and organisations to risk of prosecution | Harder to identify, and correspondingly harder to police |
| Difficulty | Easier to spot, harder to excuse | More subtle and harder to identify |

Handling conscious bias comes down to three specific actions:

1. Enforce strict anti-discrimination policies across the team.
2. Give people a route to report misconduct.
3. Act quickly on anything that raises concern.

And where the legal position is unclear: always seek advice.

## Unconscious bias: four common causes
| Cause | What it looks like |
|---|---|
| Fear | Of difference, of competition, or of failure |
| Shortcuts | Snap judgements that never get examined |
| Reluctance | Unwillingness to learn about people, to unlearn habits, or to change |
| Perceptions | Getting it wrong about what is right or what is expected |

## Bias: a project risk, not only an ethical problem
APM makes this argument explicitly, and it is the strongest framing available:

- Bias leads to unfair hiring, opportunities and advancement.
- That harms individuals and misses out on access to talent.
- It makes the workplace hostile. Instances that look trivial still leave people feeling unwelcome and undervalued, and that costs morale, productivity and welfare.
- It skews choices that affect delivery, drives stakeholders away, and can leave a situation misrepresented.
- Projects, programmes and portfolios end up at risk because of it.

Bias is a delivery risk with a named mechanism, not a soft topic bolted onto the syllabus.

## Tackling bias: the three strategies
| Strategy | What it involves |
|---|---|
| Awareness and education | Talking openly about diversity and inclusion, and bringing in expert training |
| Inclusive processes | Structure in how decisions get made, how people are hired, how communication is planned |
| Constant vigilance | Holding a culture of belonging in place through feedback, accountability and individual responsibility |

The middle one is the most practically useful. Because unconscious bias operates without awareness, good intentions cannot detect it. Only structured process can. That is why blinded CVs, capability-based role requirements and structured decision-making appear as remedies rather than 'try harder to be fair'.

And 'constant' in the third strategy is doing real work. Project professionals must constantly apply these strategies, because bias is not addressed once and closed out.

## Fairness: what it actually means
The line most likely to be misunderstood in 14c:

> Treating everyone identically is not what fairness means. Fairness means adjusting to what each person needs and prefers.

Identical treatment is not fair treatment. Someone who needs a written agenda in advance to contribute well, or a different meeting time, or a screen reader, is not being given an advantage when they get it. They are being given the same opportunity to contribute that others already had.

This maps directly onto the syllabus wording for 14c: adapting behaviours to support individuals' needs and facilitate their contributions.

## Facilitating contributions: in practice
Drawing the specific techniques together:

- Structure meetings and facilitate so everyone can contribute, and so people listen.
- Echo an unacknowledged contribution and attribute it to the speaker.
- Mentoring and sponsorship, particularly because self-promotion is less comfortable for some people.
- Allyship over advocacy where possible: help people speak for themselves rather than speaking for them, and ask first whether help is wanted and how.
- Periodic surveys to find out how people actually feel.
- Speak out when you see prejudice, discrimination or disrespect.

key_definitions.plain_english: The range of difference present in a group. Much wider than the legally protected list.
key_definitions.apm_definition: Having the broadest range of different people. It includes race and ethnicity, class, age, gender and gender identity, sexual orientation, language, mental health, religion, physical and mental ability, and neurodivergence.

key_definitions.plain_english: Making it possible for the people who are there to actually take part.
key_definitions.apm_definition: Creating an environment where everyone feels welcome.

key_definitions.plain_english: One step past inclusion. Not 'you are welcome here' but 'this is yours too'.
key_definitions.apm_definition: Making everyone feel that this is their environment. People do not feel the need to 'fit in', because the team accepts and values their differences.

key_definitions.plain_english: Using your voice for someone who is not being heard, while staying aware that it can disempower, even when well meant.
key_definitions.apm_definition: Speaking up for a group or individual who is marginalised, discriminated against, or not getting the respect they deserve.

key_definitions.plain_english: Handing over the microphone rather than using it on someone's behalf. Ask first whether help is wanted, and how.
key_definitions.apm_definition: Supporting people from marginalised groups, not by speaking for them, but by helping them secure a platform to speak for themselves.

key_definitions.plain_english: Different treatment for reasons unrelated to what someone can do.
key_definitions.apm_definition: When one person is treated more or less favourably than another. Its sources are prejudice and bias.

key_definitions.plain_english: Judging before knowing. The clue is in the word: pre-judging.
key_definitions.apm_definition: Forming an opinion before having all the relevant facts, often based on stereotypes or outdated perceptions.

key_definitions.plain_english: Leaning for or against someone for reasons that have nothing to do with the actual merits.
key_definitions.apm_definition: A preference for or against a person or their ideas without reference to their specific merits. Can be conscious (explicit) or unconscious (implicit).

key_definitions.plain_english: Bias the holder knows about and acts on anyway. Some expressions of it are illegal.
key_definitions.apm_definition: Stereotypes and attitudes that people are aware of and express deliberately, often rooted in upbringing, social conditioning, experiences and cultural norms.

key_definitions.plain_english: The bias you cannot feel operating. Which is exactly why processes rather than good intentions are the defence.
key_definitions.apm_definition: Bias arising from beliefs, stereotypes and assumptions below the level of conscious awareness, affecting selection, recognition, working relationships and decision-making without the people involved knowing it is happening.

key_definitions.plain_english: Taking the identifying details off so the assessment lands on capability.
key_definitions.apm_definition: A CV from which names, genders, ages and other personal identification have been removed before review.

body.where_this_fits: LO13 built the team; LO14 is about who is in it and whether they can actually contribute. It connects directly to LO11, where diverse thinking is the raw material for the constructive challenge that prevents groupthink, and to LO12's inclusive culture. The idea that organises the whole LO: diversity without inclusion delivers nothing. Getting different people into a room is the easy half; making it possible for them to be heard is the half that produces the performance.

14b) Understand why incorporating diversity into all parts of a project, from team members to customers, is a factor in creating a positive working environment, and understand the importance of embracing diverse thinking in teams as a means of generating innovative solutions.

14c) Understand how conscious and unconscious bias can affect actions, and know how to treat people fairly, including adapting behaviours to support individuals' needs and facilitate their contributions.

core_content.body_markdown:
## CPD: what it is
APM borrows its definition from the CIPD: CPD is the learning that develops and improves how you practise professionally.

APM frames professionalism as five things: knowledge, competence, career development, CPD and professional conduct. CPD is one of five, not the whole of it.

## CPD: the four ongoing activities
| Activity | What it involves |
|---|---|
| Identify current and future needs | Both of them: what you lack now, and what the work is about to require |
| Set learning objectives and targets | Turning a gap into something you can aim at |
| Plan activities | Supporting personal and professional development |
| Record activities and achievements | Which matters for maintaining formal status, and for knowing what you actually did |

## The CPD cycle: a repeating loop
A repeating loop rather than a list:
1. Reflection on practice: where are the gaps in what I know and what I can do?
2. Planning: how can I learn it?
3. Action: the learning, and putting it into practice.
4. Evaluation: what have I learned, and how is it benefiting my practice?

Then back to reflection. The evaluation step is the one that gets skipped, and it is the one that makes the difference: attending a course is not development until something about your practice changes.

## CPD ownership: three participants, one owner
This is the heart of 15a, because the syllabus asks specifically about the individual's role in identifying and addressing their own competence gaps.

| Participant | Their part |
|---|---|
| The learner | Takes responsibility for identifying their own competence gaps, and pursues learning or opportunities to fill them |
| The manager | Offers good performance feedback, helping set the direction for learning and development |
| The organisation | Supports CPD activities, which may include funded training or paid time off |

However, the responsibility lies firmly with each project professional. An employer who funds nothing has made your CPD harder; they have not made it someone else's problem.

## Knowledge, skills and behaviours: what CPD covers
The syllabus is explicit that CPD covers all three. Worth separating:

| Dimension | Example gap | How it gets closed |
|---|---|---|
| Knowledge | Not knowing how earned value works | Reading, courses, qualifications |
| Skills | Being unable to facilitate a workshop | Practice, coaching, doing it with support |
| Behaviours | Reacting badly to challenge | Reflection, feedback, deliberate change |

Behaviours are the hardest to self-diagnose, which is exactly why the manager's performance feedback matters. You cannot see your own shadow, to borrow LO12's phrase.

## Qualifications and accreditation: why they carry weight
Formal qualifications and accreditations carry real weight in a project professional's CPD. APM runs a structured ladder:

| Level | Qualification |
|---|---|
| Foundation | Project Fundamentals Qualification (PFQ) |
| Practitioner | Project Management Qualification (PMQ), the one you are taking |
| Advanced | Project Professional Qualification (PPQ) |
| Chartered | Chartered Project Professional (ChPP), the highest attainment of knowledge, professional practice and ethical behaviour, recorded on APM's Register of Chartered Project Professionals |

Other awarding bodies also offer qualifications, among them further and higher education institutions and other professional bodies, and project professionals often hold accreditations from more than one.

Maintaining status requires CPD: those holding formal certifications may need continuing CPD to keep them, and each professional body publishes its own CPD requirements, usually counted in CPD units, or professional development units (PDUs).

## Learning beyond courses: other ways to develop
Development works better when it reaches past courses and certificates. The sources named:

| Source | What it offers |
|---|---|
| Academic journals, e.g. *International Journal of Project Management* | Research findings |
| Practitioner magazines, e.g. *Project* | The profession in practice |
| Podcasts and YouTube channels | A mix of knowledge and opinion |
| Blogs and social media | Keeping up with trends and challenges |
| Conferences | Platforms for sharing and learning, and building contacts |

## The reflective practitioner: learning from experience
Reflective practitioners actively reflect on their experiences. They take their learning from the work rather than from pre-packaged training, mining the ordinary run of the job: what went well, what went badly, and what is still unresolved.

Note all four sources of learning in that list. Setbacks and unresolved issues count as much as successes, which connects to LO12's point that a leader must accept mistakes will happen and focus on what can be learned, and to LO6's lessons-learned reviews.

A project professional who only develops on training days is developing a few days a year. A reflective practitioner is developing continuously, from work they were doing anyway.
core_content.outcome_title: Continuing professional development and your own competence gaps

core_content.body_markdown:
## Specialist advice: why you need it at all
A single piece of project work can reach across several industries and several countries, each carrying its own laws, regulations and standards. No individual carries that in their head, and in law, ignorance is not a defence. Knowing where to get advice is itself a professional competence.

## Specialist advice: where it comes from
| Source | When used |
|---|---|
| Organisational functions | Specialists who advise the project from within the organisation. Procurement and project finance law specialists are the examples given |
| Core project team members | Where the need is constant the specialist is embedded, such as health and safety managers on a construction project |
| External legal or consultancy advice | In an unfamiliar regulatory environment, brought in from outside |
| The sponsor and governance board | They oversee and challenge project practice, provide support, and may commission expert guidance or legal support |
| Professional bodies | APM and others publish codes, frameworks and standards |

The governance route matters and links straight to LO2: if a project needs legal support it cannot fund, that is an escalation to the sponsor, not a decision to proceed uninformed.

## The hierarchy of standards: how they stack
Standards are not a flat list. They stack:

| Level | Character |
|---|---|
| Laws | Binding. Non-compliance can carry fines or custodial sentences |
| Regulations | Binding, and often industry-specific |
| International directives | Binding depending on jurisdiction |
| Government or industry guidance | Expected practice, and may be effectively mandatory in a sector |
| Discretionary standards | Adopted by choice, for example ISO 14001:2015 for environmental performance |
| Organisational policy and procedure | The organisation's own rules, sitting inside all of the above |

Codes of practice sit within many regulatory frameworks, and can be mandatory. On top of those, organisations can elect to follow discretionary standards.

## Discretionary standards: why organisations adopt them
Three named reasons:
- risk aversion
- continuous improvement
- as a marketing differentiator

A standard can be adopted for commercial positioning rather than for its content, and both are legitimate.

## Minimum compliance vs the spirit of the law: two positions
| Position | What it means |
|---|---|
| Minimum compliance | What most organisations aim for: meeting the relevant legislation and regulations |
| Beyond compliance | Some set out to meet, or better, what the law was actually trying to achieve, as part of corporate social responsibility |

Plenty of organisations also set compliance objectives explicitly, and decide how much compliance risk they will carry, with 'do no harm' a common example. That is the same deliberate-appetite thinking as risk appetite in LO1 and LO23, applied to compliance.

## Professional standards: the FIVE Dimensions

Beyond legal and regulatory standards, project professionals are held to professional ones. The APM FIVE Dimensions of Professionalism:

| Dimension | The APM artefact behind it |
|---|---|
| Breadth | The Body of Knowledge, what you need to know to run a project of any type |
| Depth | The Competence Framework, levels of knowledge and experience, mapped |
| Achievement | APM qualifications, recognised across the profession |
| Accountability | The Code of Professional Conduct, the ethical practice expected |
| Commitment | CPD |

## The Code of Professional Conduct: four areas
Four areas, and the second of them carries most of the detail:

| Area | What it covers |
|---|---|
| Professional conduct | Being competent, acting with integrity, and respecting the law, the regulations, and health, safety and environmental duties |
| Personal responsibility | Honesty, probity, confidentiality and sound judgement; serving the interests of employers and clients. Plus keeping your CPD up, declaring any interest, turning down inducements, working with due diligence, and owning what you do |
| Responsibility to the profession and the Association | Protecting and strengthening how APM and the profession are regarded |
| Ethical conduct | Doing the right thing, and raising ethical concerns when you have them |

Rejecting inducements appears here and connects directly to LO10, where the use of rewards and coercion to influence stakeholders was said to rarely have integrity. The same principle, stated as a professional obligation.

## The duty to speak up: reporting wrongdoing
Reporting wrongdoing is a professional duty, and the ethical conduct standard says so. Speaking up is everyone's obligation. The familiar word for it is whistleblowing, and that obligation runs wider than the professional body, with legal weight behind it.

What organisations must provide:

- a policy and process enabling individuals to speak up
- legal protection for people reporting suspected wrongdoing exists in many countries, the examples given being fraud or corruption, and health and safety not being safeguarded
- that protection can cover what has happened, what is happening, and what might happen, and can extend to raising concerns about a different company, one inside the project, the programme or the supply chain

What project professionals must do:

1. Build a culture ethical enough that speaking up feels safe.
2. Make sure every team member knows the route, should they need it.

Essentially, both halves are needed. A reporting process nobody feels safe using, or a safe culture where nobody knows the route, each fails on its own. Good organisations also write down a clear set of values, communicate them, and live by them at every level where decisions get made, which is the same 'best values are the ones the team sets for itself' idea from LO12.
core_content.outcome_title: Sources of specialist advice and the standards to adhere to

core_content.body_markdown:
## The legal and regulatory framework: where it comes from
Every piece of project work sits inside a legal and regulatory framework. Three things shape it: the industry involved, the country the work is done in, and the country the product ends up in.

Both locations matter. A product built in one jurisdiction and sold into another inherits obligations from both.

Understanding the regulatory environment is part of the job. The law does not accept not knowing as an excuse.

## Regulation: it changes, so monitor it
The legal and regulatory picture shifts, so you need something standing that watches for those changes. Not a one-off check at the start, but a standing arrangement, staffed by qualified and experienced experts.

This is also a live link to LO23: regulatory change is a project risk with a known likelihood of occurring, and a monitoring mechanism is the response.

## Regulation: three categories
Each category demands something different of the project.

| Category | What it requires | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Prescriptive | Specific actions the project must take | Control of substances hazardous to health |
| Competence-based | Competence of key team members to be pre-established | Roles requiring certification before work starts |
| Goal-setting | Employers set goals but decide how to meet them | Manual handling operations |

The distinction is practical. A prescriptive regulation tells you what to do. A goal-setting one leaves the method to you but still holds you to the outcome, which is harder, because there is no checklist to complete.

Some regulations are specific to the type of work, construction design and management regulations for instance. Others are relevant to all work, data privacy and safeguarding people at work among them. And some situations require team members or specialist advisors to be appropriately qualified or certified for specific pieces of work.

## The regulatory environment: what it reaches into
The syllabus asks about the impact on projects, and APM names the processes affected:

| Process | How regulation shapes it |
|---|---|
| Requirements capture | Regulatory obligations become requirements, and non-negotiable ones |
| Quality planning | Standards to be met and evidenced |
| Integrated planning | Compliance activity has to be planned and resourced |
| Scheduling | Approvals, inspections and certifications take time and sit on the critical path |
| Risk and issue management | Non-compliance is a risk, and regulatory change is a risk |
| Change control | Changes must be assessed for compliance impact, not only cost and schedule |
| Project audit and assurance | What gets audited against |

Regulation is not a separate workstream; it is a constraint threaded through the existing processes.

The syllabus also names working conditions, governance and sustainability specifically:

- Working conditions: safeguarding people at work, health and safety, and the competence requirements that go with them.
- Governance: the sponsor and board oversee and challenge project practice, and compliance sits inside the governance framework from LO2.
- Sustainability: regulatory compliance is one of the named benefits of embedding sustainability in LO3, preserving the licence to operate, and discretionary standards such as ISO 14001 are adopted to improve environmental performance.

## Non-compliance: the consequences
Breach a legally binding regulation and the organisation can face corrective action or a fine. For some breaches, an individual can go to prison.

Three factors scale the sanction:

| Factor | The question |
|---|---|
| Extent and impact | How far did the non-compliance reach, and what harm did it do? |
| Individual or systemic failure | Was this one person, or the way the organisation works? |
| How it arose | Accident, oversight, carelessness or deliberate commission |

The third factor runs on a scale of culpability: an accident and a deliberate act are treated very differently, with oversight and carelessness in between.

## Conflicting jurisdictions: when laws clash
Run a project across borders and you will eventually find two sets of rules that cannot both be satisfied.

The answer: which standard the project aligns to is settled by the governance structure, on specialist advice where that is needed.

It is a governance decision, informed by specialist advice, and that is the same delegated-authority principle as LO2, applied to a decision that exceeds the project's competence as well as its authority.
core_content.outcome_title: How the legal and regulatory landscape affects projects

worked_examples.ask: Do you wait for an inspector to tell you what to install?
worked_examples.answer: No. Goal-setting regulation leaves the method to you and still holds you to the outcome, so the assessment, the lifting aids and the training are yours to choose and yours to evidence. No checklist discharges it for you.
worked_examples.heading: Regulation: three categories
worked_examples.situation: Manual handling on your fit-out site is hurting people. The regulation sets the goal and names no method.

worked_examples.ask: Is that a cost and schedule decision?
worked_examples.answer: No. Every change gets assessed for compliance impact as well, and cladding sits under building regulations. Approve it on cost and programme alone and you have taken a regulatory risk the board never saw, which is what change control exists to catch.
worked_examples.heading: The regulatory environment: what it reaches into
worked_examples.situation: A supplier offers cheaper cladding that saves 48,000 pounds and two weeks. Your change board meets Thursday.

key_definitions.plain_english: Knowing your job, keeping that knowledge current, and behaving properly while doing it.
key_definitions.apm_definition: A commitment to developing and maintaining the highest standards of competence and integrity. APM frames it as five things: knowledge, competence, career development, continuing professional development and professional conduct.

key_definitions.plain_english: Deliberately staying good at your job. Planned and recorded, not just whatever happened to come up.
key_definitions.apm_definition: Learning experiences which help you develop and improve your professional practice (CIPD). It involves identifying current and future needs, setting learning objectives, planning development activities, and recording activities and achievements.

key_definitions.plain_english: Someone who learns from the work itself, not only from courses about the work.
key_definitions.apm_definition: Someone who actively reflects on their experiences, finding learning opportunities in daily experiences, successes, setbacks and unresolved issues rather than relying on digested knowledge such as training.

key_definitions.plain_english: Five things a professional is measured on, each with an APM artefact behind it.
key_definitions.apm_definition: A framework of standards guiding the development of project professionals: breadth (Body of Knowledge), depth (Competence Framework), achievement (qualifications), accountability (Code of Professional Conduct) and commitment (CPD).

key_definitions.plain_english: The rulebook for behaviour. Accountability is the dimension of professionalism it sits under.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The code setting standards for project professionals in four areas: professional conduct, personal responsibility, responsibility to the profession and the Association, and ethical conduct.

key_definitions.plain_english: A standard you choose to meet. Nobody makes you; you do it because it is worth doing or worth being seen to do.
key_definitions.apm_definition: An international or industry standard an organisation elects to follow rather than being required to, adopted for reasons including risk aversion, continuous improvement or as a marketing differentiator. An example is ISO 14001:2015 for environmental performance.

key_definitions.plain_english: Meeting the intention behind a rule rather than the minimum the rule technically requires.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The basis on which some organisations go beyond minimum compliance, aiming to achieve or exceed the spirit of the law rather than just its letter.

key_definitions.plain_english: How close to the legal line the organisation is willing to operate. Set deliberately, not by accident.
key_definitions.apm_definition: An organisation's defined appetite for compliance risk, alongside specific compliance objectives. A common example is a desire to 'do no harm'.

key_definitions.plain_english: Reporting wrongdoing. A duty rather than an option, and protected by law in many countries.
key_definitions.apm_definition: Speaking up to report any form of wrongdoing. A professional duty under the ethical conduct standard, with responsibilities extending beyond the professional body and carrying wider legal implications.

body.where_this_fits: This is the LO about the project professional rather than the project. It connects to LO14 (the duty to speak out when you see discrimination), LO3 (responsible project management and CSR), LO2 (the sponsor and board who oversee compliance) and LO23 (regulatory change as a risk). The single idea running through it: responsibility sits with the individual. Your employer supports your CPD but does not own it, and 'I did not know the regulation existed' is not a defence in law.
learning_outcomes: 15a) Understand the importance of continuing professional development, which should cover both knowledge, skills and behaviours, and the individual's role in identifying and addressing their own competence gaps.
15b) Knowledge of the sources of specialist advice and standards that need to be adhered to.
15c) Understand the impact of the legal and regulatory landscape on projects (such as the impact on working conditions, risk management, governance and sustainability).

core_content.body_markdown:
## Requirements management: what it is for
It means finding out what stakeholders want and need, working out which of it holds up, and ranking what remains. Requirements that are both thorough and achievable become the yardstick the project gets measured against. They shape the benefits, the objectives, and the acceptance criteria.

Requirements and scope are inseparable. The scope is the work to be done, and you cannot describe it without first knowing what the stakeholders are asking the project for. Neither exists without the other. That is the direct answer to how requirements management establishes scope.

## Requirements: how they evolve through the life cycle
| Stage | What requirements do |
|---|---|
| Early life cycle | High-level requirements show how the change aligns with organisational strategy and help define what success looks like. They help sponsoring stakeholders draw out the benefits, confirming they are realistic, attainable and measurable, feeding early decision-making and the business case |
| As the project progresses | Finer-grained requirements emerge as project professionals work alongside subject-matter experts, defining objectives and acceptance criteria and linking back to the identified benefits and success criteria |

Rigour varies by life cycle. Heavy rigour up front suits some projects; others do better letting requirements evolve. It is the same linear-versus-iterative split as everywhere else.

## Success criteria vs benefits: two different things
Two different things, measured at different moments, owned by different people.

| | Success criteria | Benefits |
|---|---|---|
| What | The satisfaction of stakeholder needs, measured against criteria agreed at the start | Positive and measurable improvements delivered by change, focused on strategic intent |
| Example | An office building is refurbished | Maintenance costs fall (tangible); staff morale improves (intangible) |
| When known | At project handover | Often only once the product is adopted and embedded into business as usual (in a linear life cycle) |
| Accountable | The project manager | The project sponsor |

And the consequence: a project can deliver its success criteria and fail to deliver the benefits. The reverse happens too. Benefits land, yet the project is remembered as a failure. The two are measured separately, so they can diverge.

Stakeholders may have different views of success. The project professional's role is to:

- draw out how different people are defining success and benefit
- broker a shared position, so far as one is available

'As far as possible' is doing real work there. Total agreement is not always available, and the job is to get as close as the situation allows and make the remaining differences visible.

Success criteria can change, but only subject to formal approval, which means change control, per LO24. In an iterative environment, shifting success criteria are easier to absorb, because steady contact with end users lets the team learn and adapt as it goes.

## Good requirements: what makes them
Project professionals ensure that:

- benefits, success criteria, objectives and requirements all connect visibly to each other
- the objectives are spelled out, and stakeholders have agreed them
- each requirement is unambiguous, and put as plainly as it can be

That chain, benefits then success criteria then objectives then requirements, is worth memorising as a chain. Every requirement should be traceable back up it.

The test is SMART.

| Letter | Meaning |
|---|---|
| S | Specific |
| M | Measurable |
| A | Achievable |
| R | Relevant |
| T | Time-based |

Measures make acceptance possible. APM's example: a requirement (speed of ship) plus a measure (greater than 12 knots) is what lets a deliverable be accepted when it transfers to users. A requirement without a measure cannot be accepted or rejected. It can only be argued about.

Not everything measures easily. A benefit the sponsor wants can generate a requirement that resists easy measurement. The example given is delivering the work in an environmentally sustainable way. Acknowledging that difficulty is better than pretending a soft requirement is hard.

## Requirements management: the four-step process
The process first establishes a requirements baseline, then regularly reviews it.

| Step | What happens |
|---|---|
| 1. Identify stakeholders and gather requirements | Work out who the stakeholders are by looking at which parts of the business gain from the change or are hit by it. Settle how you will capture requirements (workshops, surveys), then go and get their first view |
| 2. Analyse, validate and align | A proposed requirement is not automatically accepted. Analyse thoroughly for dependencies, risks and constraints; validate each one; check it aligns with project objectives and contributes to broader organisational aims |
| 3. Prioritise | The list almost always exceeds what can be built. Use MoSCoW, ranking on value, benefit, cost, risk and size. Stakeholders agree the prioritisation, and the initial baseline is set |
| 4. Review and reprioritise regularly | As more information emerges, review and reprioritise. New requirements follow the same analysis, validation and alignment before being consolidated into an updated baseline |

The syllabus phrases this as gather, analysis, justifying requirements and baseline needs. Those are the same four steps under different labels. 'Justifying' is step 2's validation: proving a requirement earns its place.

Stakeholders propose; the project analyses and validates. A requirements process that records what people asked for and stops there has skipped its most valuable step.

## MoSCoW: prioritising requirements
| Category | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Must have | Non-negotiable, because the project fails without it |
| Should have | Important but not vital; there is a workaround |
| Could have | Desirable; included if capacity allows |
| Won't have | Explicitly excluded this time |

The fourth category is the useful one. Won't have is a decision that was taken and recorded, not a requirement that got lost, and recording it prevents the requirement reappearing later as an assumed inclusion.

## Requirement reviews: when they happen
Frequency should be project-specific, though in practice they cluster around the moments that already matter: a stage gate, the end of an iteration, reusing existing control points, as LO4 and LO6 recommend.

It runs for the whole life cycle, absorbing information that surfaces later and needs that shift as it goes.

And the handover to 16b: when requirements change or new ones are introduced, they have to be brought into line with the configuration management and change management processes, so governance, control and the decision itself all happen properly.

## Requirements and acceptance: the V model

Defining a requirement and designing the test that will judge it are the same act viewed from two ends. The 'V' depiction of the life cycle shows this: requirements descend the left-hand side from user requirements through system requirements to design and build; testing ascends the right-hand side, with each test level verifying or validating its counterpart on the left.

Why the rigour matters commercially: the level of rigour mitigates the risk of a later dispute about acceptance and transition of deliverables into use. For projects delivered under a commercial contract this is particularly important, safeguarding both the investing and supplier organisations. That is the LO5 link. It is more achievable when the project is well understood and the commercial setting is steady, which is precisely why uncertain projects need a different approach.

## Iterative life cycles: how requirements work
Requirements get surfaced, then sharpened through analysis until everyone agrees what is meant. Some methods write them as user stories: a feature a stakeholder has asked for, written in ordinary language, carrying only enough detail to size the development effort roughly.

That last phrase is the point of a user story. It is deliberately not a specification; it carries enough to estimate and to start a conversation.

core_content.body_markdown:
## Configuration management: what it does
It is the technical and administrative work of creating, maintaining, controlling changes to, and quality-checking the project's technical configuration.

Done well, it delivers two things: accuracy and alignment of the latest configuration, and clear traceability between versions.

Why it exists: on a technical project, what change control approves lands straight in the specification of what gets built. Once a change is agreed it must be written into the project's configuration, so that any change to the functional and physical characteristics of a deliverable is documented and communicated to the entire team.

Without it, a change is approved and half the team keeps building to the old specification.

## Configuration management: it scales with complexity
| Complexity | What configuration management looks like |
|---|---|
| Simplest | Version control of documents and information, keeping changes and knowledge up to date, which is the LO6 information management link |
| More complex | Designs that are many-sided, pull in several technical disciplines, and cover a spread of different assets |
| Most complex | Asset control, keeping every asset's configuration within organisational and regulatory standards |

Business information modelling (BIM) sits alongside it: digital representations of physical assets, created and maintained. Those models make a complicated configuration visible and let people decide about a technical asset such as a building or an aircraft.

## Configuration management: the five steps
The syllabus names these explicitly: planning, identification, control, status accounting, verification audit. Learn what each one does.

| Step | What it involves |
|---|---|
| 1. Configuration management planning | A configuration management plan describing the project-specific procedures, how they are applied and who completes them. The worked example is how a construction project's technical designs get updated and issued |
| 2. Configuration identification | Break the project into configuration items, giving each a unique number or reference. That becomes the first baseline, and the one place the truth lives |
| 3. Configuration control | Once change control has approved something, this is what gets it into the current configuration version, including updating any dependencies between configuration items that the change disturbs |
| 4. Configuration status accounting | Regular reporting on the configuration's status, so everyone has the most up-to-date information, and keeping each configuration item traceable across its whole development |
| 5. Configuration verification audits | Check the deliverable matches the configuration on record. Usually run as a phase closes, once a deliverable is complete, or as the output passes into use |

Step 3 is where the two processes meet. Configuration control does not approve changes; change control does that (LO24). Configuration control makes sure an approved change lands in the record.

Step 3 also carries an easily-missed detail: interrelationships between configuration items get updated too. Changing one component can invalidate another that depended on it.

## Requirements vs configuration management: how they divide the work
The cleanest way to hold 16a and 16b together:

| | Requirements management | Configuration management |
|---|---|---|
| Job | Establishes scope | Manages and controls scope |
| Question it answers | What are we building, and why? | What exactly is it right now, and how did it get that way? |
| Output | An agreed, prioritised requirements baseline | An accurate, traceable configuration |
| When | Heaviest early, continuing throughout | Throughout delivery, into transition |

## Verification audits: where they sit
The timing of step 5 connects to three other LOs at once:

- At the end of a life cycle phase, alongside the decision gates of LO6.
- When a deliverable is finished, supporting the quality and acceptance work of LO18.
- As the output passes into use. That is the acceptance sequence of LO8, where deliverables are tested against acceptance criteria before the sponsor signs off.

That last one closes the loop opened in 16a. Requirements defined a measure; the V model designed a test against it; configuration management recorded what was actually built; and the verification audit confirms the built thing matches the documented configuration before it is handed over.

## Requirement changes: governance applies
As covered in 16a: a changed or newly-arrived requirement has to be run through configuration management and change management, so that governance, control and the decision itself all happen properly.

A new requirement is not added straight to a list. It goes through analysis, validation and alignment; it is prioritised against everything already there; it goes through change control if it affects an approved baseline; and it lands in the configuration record.

body.where_this_fits: LO16 opens the delivery half of the course, and it is where the abstract becomes concrete: benefits and success criteria from LO4 and LO9 turn into requirements you can build against and test. Two processes, cleanly split. Requirements management *establishes* scope; configuration management *controls* it once established. The distinction the exam most wants: success criteria and benefits are not the same thing, and a project can hit one while missing the other.
learning_outcomes: 16a) Understand how to establish scope through requirements management processes (such as gather, analysis, justifying requirements and baseline needs).
16b) Understand how to manage scope through configuration management processes (such as planning, identification, control, status accounting and verification audit).

core_content.body_markdown:
## Solutions development: where it starts
Requirements management dealt with what stakeholders need or want to be able to do. Solutions development explores how to meet them, determining the optimal solution to satisfy the agreed requirements.

It begins by getting clear on what problem is actually being solved, which forces you to rank the competing requirements different stakeholders brought. From there the team produces several options and works through them before settling on one, and that choice then goes through refinement and change control.

It mixes two modes of thinking: finding options needs creative thinking, good facilitation and technical expertise, while choosing between them needs rigorous analysis to find the option offering greatest value.

## Functional and non-functional requirements: solutions must meet both
| Type | What it covers |
|---|---|
| Functional | The things it has to be able to do |
| Non-functional | The qualities it must have: how it looks, how long it lasts, how sustainable, reliable, secure and safe it is, how it performs, how it is maintained |

Non-functional requirements are the ones that get under-specified and then become acceptance disputes. A solution that does everything asked of it but cannot be maintained has failed a real requirement.

## Exploring options: build in the time
Carve out time at the start purely for producing options and alternatives. APM is blunt about why: too often there is a rush to solutions.

On a larger, more complex project, dedicating a phase to option generation demonstrates good governance and improves transparency, clarifying to others why the eventual approach was taken.

## Framing: it determines what options exist
The single most useful idea in LO17, best learned through APM's own example:

| Framing | Options it permits |
|---|---|
| 'Build a bridge between A and B' | Location and type of bridge |
| 'Facilitate the movement of people between A and B' | Bridge, tunnel, ferry, relocating the destination, removing the need to travel |

Frame it as the problem needing solved, and the outcomes you want and the benefits behind them follow naturally from there. Frame it as a solution and you have chosen before you started.

## Option dimensions: what options should cover
| Dimension | The question |
|---|---|
| Doing nothing | What happens if we do not proceed? Always an option |
| Minimum viable solution to complete solution | How much of the possible scope do we build? |
| Single-phased or multi-phased | Do we do it in one pass or several? |
| Level of technology maturity | How proven does the technology need to be? |

On minimum viable solution: it should always be considered as an option. It is the cheapest and quickest to deliver, and makes designers work out the least that has to be true for the project to have succeeded at all. However, stakeholders may want to go further and add features for greater benefits in the longer term.

On phasing: a simple short project can be single-phase. More complicated ones need thought. Should there be a pilot for proof of concept? Should it be trialled in one area, evaluated, and rolled out once the lessons are in? Or does the clock, or a need to show commitment across the board, force it all into one phase? And where the details are not known at the outset, a discovery phase may be needed to reach full clarity, after which the project is either terminated or replanned in light of what was learned.

On technology maturity: most stakeholders dislike depending on ageing technology, but anything not yet properly proven, or whose standards are still unsettled, deserves an argument before it is adopted. Different options carry different risks.

On the strategic dimension: starting a project cuts off other options and future opportunities. Some options allow a wider variety of future opportunities; others take the organisation down a tightly defined path. So projects must be considered in line with the organisation's broader strategic direction, not evaluated in isolation, which is the LO4 and LO9 link.

## Option evaluation: how it works
Working every option up into a full solution is not realistic, but each should at least be named and roughly assessed, leaving a shortlist worth pursuing. Assess on:

- what the project is for, meaning the problem being solved
- what it does for the organisation's future
- the risk it carries, and how likely it is to succeed or fail
- whether we can deliver it
- cost, time and quality, as always

The critical sequencing point: the assessment holds up best when the criteria were settled with stakeholders before anyone listed an option. Criteria written after the options are on the table can be shaped, consciously or not, to favour a preferred answer.

Criteria might take in a cost-benefit analysis tied back to the business case, plus impacts that are commercial, operational, technical, environmental and strategic.

## Solutions development: the six-component process
| Step | What happens |
|---|---|
| 1. Identify options | More options increase the likelihood of project success. Engage the team to research and think creatively. Every option has to speak to what stakeholders have prioritised and be able to return value to the organisation funding it |
| 2. Evaluate options | Against criteria agreed with stakeholders beforehand |
| 3. Select | The best option to meet requirements and deliver value |
| 4. Governance framework | Wraps the whole process. Document the option selected, the decision process followed, and the specification for the solution, then communicate the choice to stakeholders |
| 5. Monitoring | A monitoring and control cycle during delivery, including quality assurance and quality control. Run plan-do-check-act, the Shewhart cycle, to adjust the process and tighten efficiency. Decide what data to collect to understand progress and anticipate issues |
| 6. Change control | Ensures all requests for change to features or functionality get a robust assessment. Once approved, record the new solution configuration in full and tell stakeholders what changed |

It ends with sign-off ahead of handover, the final piece of governance in the process.

## Scope: turning the solution into it
With a solution chosen, develop a scope that articulates its parts, aiming to maximise clarity and minimise ambiguity.

In scope and out of scope both get stated. Recording assumptions and exclusions is the main lever for mitigating the risk of scope creep. APM's examples of exclusions: transition resources drawn from BAU rather than funded by the project; customised reporting in a software implementation; ground-source heating left out of a building refurbishment.

Stating both sides cuts the risk of misunderstanding and gives you something to judge change requests against. Scope defined badly is a well-known route to delay, cost overrun and benefits that never arrive.

Interfaces matter too. Understanding interfaces with other work is critical to avoid duplication, conflicts or omission, whether that is inside a programme or portfolio, across to other standalone projects, or against BAU work.

## Breakdown structures: the four to know
In linear life cycles, breakdown structures formally define scope:

| Structure | Defines |
|---|---|
| PBS (product breakdown structure) | Things to create |
| WBS (work breakdown structure) | Activities to complete |
| OBS (organisation breakdown structure) | Allocation of people |
| CBS (cost breakdown structure) | Project budget |

A work package is the part of a WBS allocated to a team member. Combining the WBS and OBS produces the responsibility assignment matrix, which is the LO2 link.

## Linear vs iterative: how scope is defined
This is the distinction the exam wants.

| | Linear | Iterative |
|---|---|---|
| When scope is fixed | Approval of the scope definition fixes it. Planning then optimises time, cost and quality | Solutions selected and scope fixed later, and in stages |
| How scope is held | Breakdown structures | A product backlog of potential scope elements, often as user stories |
| How scope changes | Only through formal change control | The team draws down the highest-priority items each iteration |
| When it stops | At the agreed scope | Iterations keep adding until the next increment of benefit costs more than it returns |

Iterative approaches identify options in much the same way, and the difference is when they commit. Deferring the commitment suits situations where committing early would be a mistake:

- requirements that keep moving
- technology still under development
- a build process you expect to learn from

Stop when the next increment costs more than it returns, an economic rule rather than a fixed list.

## MVP and MMP: two different questions
The syllabus names both. They answer different questions.

| | Minimum viable product (MVP) | Minimum marketable product (MMP) |
|---|---|---|
| Question | What is the smallest thing that works and lets us learn? | What is the smallest thing customers would accept or pay for? |
| Purpose | Validate assumptions, gather feedback, reduce wasted build | Reach the market, or reach real users, with the least scope necessary |
| Audience | Often internal or a limited user group | The market or the full user base |
| Risk it addresses | Building the wrong thing | Building more than the market needed before earning anything back |

How they work together in an iterative life cycle: early iterations produce an MVP to test whether the solution is right at all. Later iterations build towards an MMP, the point at which the output is good enough to release and start generating outcomes and benefits. Iterations carry on past that point, adding value right up until the next increment stops paying for itself.

This connects straight to LO1 and LO9: iterative projects realise benefits incrementally, and the MMP is the point where that realisation can begin.

MVP comes from the APM Body of Knowledge. MMP does not: it is standard iterative practice that the syllabus names, so present it as general practice rather than APM content.

core_content.body_markdown:
## Phases: why projects are structured this way
Phases exist for three reasons, and it pays to learn them as three named reasons rather than a vague sense that phases are tidy.

| Reason | What it buys you |
|---|---|
| Better grouping of activities | Phases group work by type (analysis, planning, building) so the right people are on the right kind of work at the right time. |
| More accurate plans and estimates | Smaller chunks are easier to plan and estimate, which raises both accuracy and confidence. |
| Tracking and monitoring progress | Phases create clear break points to measure against checkpoints and milestones, so you can see early whether things are on track. |

Every project passes through the same high-level phases whichever life cycle is used. The life cycle decides *how* you move through them, not whether they exist.

## Life cycle approaches: only two at the top level
There are only two at the top level. Everything else blends them.

Linear runs distinct, sequential phases in a single pass. You move on only once the current phase is complete.

Iterative runs repeatable phases. You create an initial output, then build on it with further deliveries of incremental value as the solution evolves.

Hybrid is a deliberate blend, because most real environments are messy enough that neither pure approach fits end to end.

## Linear: the phases, and the control they buy

Because each phase finishes before the next begins, linear gives tight control over progression and a clear framework for scheduling, budgeting, resourcing and risk.

The boundaries matter as much as the phases. Gateways are what they create, and a gateway is where milestones, governance and reviews live. No gateway, nowhere to put the decision.

| Phase | What happens |
|---|---|
| Concept | An idea (exploiting an opportunity or solving a problem) is analysed for viability and fit with organisational objectives. Research, high-level requirements, often an outline business case. |
| Definition | How to make it real is planned: detailed analysis, estimation, planning and a fuller statement of requirements, ending in the sponsor's approval to proceed. |
| Deployment | Plans are implemented. Testing and assurance monitor performance to keep intended outcomes and benefits on track. |
| Transition | Outputs are accepted and transitioned into use, handover, then formal closure. |

Naming and phasing vary by organisation, shaped by its nature, purpose, environment and governance culture. Smaller projects often use a shorter cycle.

Fits best: clearly defined or high-risk projects, where time, cost and risk can flex to protect agreed scope and quality, and projects with a high cost of change, where extra rigour up front pays for itself.

## Iterative: how it actually works

Iterative rests on continuous improvement and evolutionary development: the solution evolves as learning takes place and new information emerges.

You start with a high-level vision. Detail is defined and built inside each cycle. Because specification and design run in parallel, deployment is fast-tracked and users get value earlier, which produces rapid feedback you can act on.

A common structure comes from the dynamic systems development method (DSDM):

| Phase | What happens |
|---|---|
| Pre-project and feasibility | The idea is established, aligned to objectives, cost effective, technically possible, with a clear measurable goal. |
| Foundations | Planning and design: a high-level delivery plan and a technical design. |
| Evolutionary development and deployment | Repeatable cycles of detailed design, development, testing and deployment. Early cycles produce an initial output; later ones add value as learning emerges. |
| Realisation | Embed the outputs and evolve the next iteration. |

Many iterative life cycles use sprints: timeboxed iterations with a fixed end date, typically producing a minimum viable product first, with further scope assessed, prioritised and planned into later iterations. A daily scrum keeps the team synchronised.

Fits best: new or innovative work without detailed up-front knowledge, prototypes and pioneering technology, and situations with a low cost of change so the project can pivot quickly.

What it demands: collaboration and co-creation. It runs on engagement and regular feedback from end users, and works best with co-located teams, which keeps communication barriers down.

## Hybrid: blending the two

There is no one-size-fits-all life cycle. A hybrid takes the useful parts of each for a specific project.

The common pattern: iterative through concept and definition to work through early uncertainty, then linear for deployment and transition once there is clarity. Stakeholders get certainty on scope; the project gets structure for controlling schedule, budget, quality and risk.

You are not locked in. Many successful projects adapt as they go.

What makes hybrid work or fail is alignment with the organisation's wider governance, reporting, change control, roles and responsibilities, and dependencies on other initiatives. Blend the life cycles without aligning governance and you get two systems of working arguing with each other.

core_content.body_markdown:
## Project vs extended life cycle: where each one stops
A standard project life cycle ends once the agreed outputs are deployed and handed over. An extended life cycle adds two phases on the end.

| Added phase | What it covers |
|---|---|
| Adoption | Communications, training, knowledge sharing and change management, so operational teams actually use the outputs correctly. |
| Benefits realisation | Measuring business performance to confirm adoption is producing the intended outcomes and the anticipated benefits. |

They typically run in parallel, not one after the other. As adoption rises, outcomes improve, and benefits follow.

## Outputs, outcomes and benefits: the chain that connects them
> A new software tool is delivered (output), customer usage increases (outcome), service delivery costs fall (benefit).

Delivering the output guarantees none of the rest. That is the entire argument for extending.

## Benefits measurement: how it actually happens
This is what the extra phases actually do:

- Benefits planning is where the groundwork is laid, early rather than at the end: activities and resources for transition into use, testing schedules, acceptance criteria, quality assurance thresholds.
- Benefit owners and change managers stay active for the project's whole duration, readying the business to take the outputs.
- Measurement varies by benefit type: quantitative for operational and financial benefits, qualitative (such as user feedback) for non-financial ones.
- The project sponsor is ultimately accountable for the measurement process being robust, usually through formal benefits realisation reviews.
- If benefits are not landing, there are two honest moves: drive adoption harder, or reset the target.

## Benefits timing: how it differs by life cycle
Benefits do not arrive at the same point in every life cycle:

- Linear: benefits are usually realised at the end, once all outputs are delivered.
- Iterative: benefits are realised incrementally, as the project progresses.

## Extending the life cycle: when it makes sense
Programmes normally include adoption and benefits realisation as standard. For a standalone project it is a real trade-off:

| For extending | Against extending |
|---|---|
| Higher adoption rates | The organisation pays for project professionals' time on those activities |
| Better chance the benefits are realised, often what stakeholders judge success on | Operational teams could manage it instead |
| The project team learns how their work actually lands in the business | |

A project inside a larger programme may only need to deliver outputs, because the programme handles adoption and benefits.

Timing matters. If you are going to extend, plan for it in the early phases: the requirements, work, resources and risks of the extra phases all belong in the project management plan from the start.
