core_content.body_markdown:
## Integrated planning: the core argument
Integrated planning exists to line up every component of the project so that stakeholders can believe the business case will be delivered.

That single sentence answers 19b. Everything below expands it.

## Integration: why it matters specifically
The components of a project are not independent. APM makes the point through dependencies, and it generalises:

> The parts are related. Move one and another moves with it, whether you intended that or not.

So a project with a schedule plan, a cost plan and a resource plan that were produced separately does not have three plans. It has three claims that have never been tested against each other. Integration is what turns them into one statement about what will happen.

The plan's job is to get each part arriving at the moment it is needed, which is what gives the project its best chance.

## A PMP: what producing one achieves
| Benefit | Why it follows |
|---|---|
| Confidence the business case is achievable | The stated aim. The PMP is the evidence that the promise in LO4 can be delivered |
| Sign-off becomes possible | Robust estimation, dependency management and risk identification give stakeholders the initial confidence to sign off and proceed |
| A single view for governance | Everything important, in one summary a steering committee or governance board can use, which is the LO2 link |
| A baseline for progress monitoring | The deployment baseline is the starting point for progress monitoring |
| A basis for assessing change | Change control assesses requests against the baseline (LO24). Without an integrated baseline, the impact of a change cannot be traced across components |
| Control demonstrated during delivery | Component-level data is collected and watched, which is how control gets evidenced |
| Boundaries reconfirmed | Approval is when you re-examine what is in scope, what is out, and where the project touches other projects and BAU |
| Contingency held deliberately | Resources solely reserved for risk response, rather than discovered to be missing later |

## Not integrating: the consequence
APM gives one consequence directly, about dependencies, and it stands for the whole:

Dependencies left unmanaged stop projects, force a replan, push costs up, and push the benefits back.

Pause, replan, cost more, deliver benefits later. That is the failure mode integration prevents, and it is a better scenario answer than a general appeal to good practice.

## Integration: it continues after approval
A PMP produced once and filed is not integrated planning. It is a document. The work continues:

- As things move and information arrives, keep watching the plan through data on each component.
- The agreed governance forums are where progress gets reported and contingency gets released when things slip.
- Estimating is continuous, and updated estimates feed into change control, driving adjustments to the integrated plan.
- Dependencies are managed through regular review and replanning.
- Risk identification continues throughout, as the project evolves and new stakeholders arrive.

Notice the pattern: every constituent process feeds back into the integrated plan. That is what makes it integrated rather than assembled.

## The first integrated plan: why it is hard, and what makes it possible
Producing that first integrated plan is hard, and it needs a lot of people to contribute. Acknowledging the difficulty is part of a good answer, since the three techniques exist precisely because it is hard:

| Technique | What it contributes |
|---|---|
| Robust estimation | Numbers stakeholders can believe, with assumptions visible |
| Dependency management | A sequence that can happen |
| Risk identification | Honesty about what could go wrong, and contingency sized for it |

## Plan assurance: the integrated baseline review
Good practice is an integrated baseline review completed by an independent reviewer, a risk-based check that the deployment baseline is achievable inside the budget and the schedule it claims.

Worth noticing what that implies. The plan is important enough to warrant independent assurance in its own right, before any delivery has happened. A plan nobody has challenged is a plan whose optimism has not been tested.

## The honest framing: two things to hold together
Two things to hold together, because scenario questions often set them against each other:

- Plans will change. Issues arise, information emerges, estimates are revised.
- That does not reduce the need to plan well. APM says it plainly of linear projects: problems will arise regardless, and that is no reason to plan any less carefully before starting.

The integrated plan is not a prediction that must come true. It is the current best statement of how the project delivers its business case: maintained, monitored and revised through governance as reality arrives.

worked_examples.answer: Change control assesses the request against the baseline. With scope, schedule, cost and resources baselined together, you can trace two languages through all four. Separate plans give you four unlinked guesses.

misconceptions.wrong: An integrated project management plan is a folder containing all the project's plans.

key_definitions.plain_english: Pulling every separate plan into one that actually agrees with itself.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The process of collecting, aligning and managing a suite of constituent plans that come together to create a holistic project management plan.

key_definitions.plain_english: The single document that says what the project is doing, by when, for how much, with whom, and what could go wrong.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The holistic plan aligning all components of a successful project, succinctly summarising all key project information for use in forums such as a steering committee or governance board.

key_definitions.plain_english: Predicting what it will take. Always a prediction, but a disciplined one.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The process of forecasting the time, resource and costs required to deliver the project's scope to the agreed level of quality.

key_definitions.plain_english: Estimating the whole from the outside in, using history or comparison.
key_definitions.apm_definition: Estimating from a high-level view when detailed information is not available, using parametric or analogous methods. Useful in the early stages of the life cycle.

key_definitions.plain_english: Estimating the parts and adding them up. Slower, more accurate, needs detail you may not have yet.
key_definitions.apm_definition: Estimating by breaking the project into parts and estimating each in detail, using analytical or Delphi methods. Often used to validate top-down estimates as more information becomes available.

key_definitions.plain_english: Best case, worst case, most likely. The number carries its own uncertainty with it.
key_definitions.apm_definition: An estimating approach determining a range, from which an informed opinion is given on the most likely estimate within that range, noting any estimating assumptions made.

key_definitions.plain_english: One thing having to wait for another. The reason a plan is a network rather than a list.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The relationship between activities and resources within a project, where the ability for a task to start or finish depends on the completion of another.

key_definitions.plain_english: Keeping track of what waits for what, so nothing stalls unexpectedly.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The process of identifying, planning and managing a project's interrelated tasks and resources.

key_definitions.plain_english: Because of this, that might happen, and it would do this to us. Three parts, always.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The structure for describing a risk clearly: cause being environmental factors that may create uncertainty, event being situations that may occur within or around the project, and impact being the effect on one or more project objectives.

key_definitions.plain_english: Money and time held back deliberately, so a foreseeable problem does not become a crisis.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The process of setting aside resources solely reserved for responding to risks and uncertainty, bridging the gap that risk creates.

key_definitions.plain_english: The agreed version of the plan that delivery gets measured against.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The plan for the execution of the project, supporting the integrated project management plan, setting out baseline plans for scope, timeline, quality and budget. Approved at the decision gate before the deployment phase.

body.where_this_fits: This is the LO where everything else converges. Scope from LO17, quality from LO18, schedule from LO20, resources from LO21, budget from LO22, risk from LO23. Each has its own plan, and integrated planning is what makes them one coherent document rather than six that contradict each other. The word doing the work is *integrated*: the point is not that plans exist, it is that they align.

core_content.body_markdown:
## Scope: three things, not one
As covered in LO17: scope covers the whole of what the project produces (outputs, outcomes and benefits) together with the work needed to produce it.

| Element | What it is | Who it belongs to |
|---|---|---|
| Output | The thing the project creates | Project manager delivers it |
| Outcome | What changes because the output is used | Arrives through adoption |
| Benefit | The measurable improvement that change produces | Sponsor is accountable |

A schedule built only around outputs will finish at handover and leave the outcomes and benefits unscheduled, which is exactly the failure LO8 and LO9 describe. Where an extended life cycle is used, adoption and benefits realisation are scheduled work too.

## Breakdown structures: turning scope into a schedule
Breakdown structures are what convert scope into something you can put dates against. The syllabus names three for 20a; the fourth completes the set.

| Structure | Defines | Feeds |
|---|---|---|
| PBS, the product breakdown structure | The things to create: scope expressed as products | The WBS |
| WBS, the work breakdown structure | The activities to complete to deliver those products | The schedule and the RAM |
| CBS, the cost breakdown structure | The project budget | LO22 |
| OBS, the organisation breakdown structure | The allocation of people | The RAM, LO21 |

The sequence matters. Products first, then the work needed to produce them. Building a WBS without a PBS produces a list of activities nobody can trace to a deliverable.

A work package is the slice of the WBS handed to one team member by whoever manages the project or programme. It is the unit that gets estimated, scheduled and tracked.

WBS plus OBS gives you the responsibility assignment matrix, setting out every item of work, who is on it, and what part each of them plays (LO2, LO21).

## From breakdown to schedule: the steps
1. Decompose scope into products (PBS), then activities (WBS).
2. Agree the dependencies between activities: logical, preferential and resource (LO19).
3. Estimate durations, ideally as three-point estimates: the optimistic case, the pessimistic case, and the point in between judged most likely.
4. Build the precedence network from the dependency logic.
5. Run critical path analysis to find the duration, the critical path and the float.
6. Present it, usually as a Gantt chart showing activities as bars on a timeline.

Estimates of duration are based on effort, which is why LO19's estimating methods sit underneath this LO.

## Schedule levels: different resolutions
Schedules come at different levels of resolution, anything from a single-page plan up to a full control schedule. Big or complicated projects often run several at once, each covering a different aspect, with one master schedule pulling them together, coordinating them and tracking them.

Rolling wave is common for linear projects: near-term activities in detail, later stages at a higher level. It is an honest response to the fact that distant detail is guesswork.

## The schedule: what it is for
The schedule is how you demonstrate that the timeline is deliverable. It settles what the project team and the customer are each expecting, and everything monitored later gets measured against it.

The resulting timeline forms an important part of the deployment baseline, documented in enough detail to inform the direction of work and the monitoring of progress.

core_content.body_markdown:
## Dependency and link types: what the schedule is built on
From LO19, because the schedule is built on them:

| Dependency type | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Logical / hard | Cannot start until another has started or finished |
| Preferential / soft | Should not start: the delay is driven by governance, process or quality control |
| Resource | Cannot start because the same resource is in use elsewhere |

Link types in the network:

| Link | Constraint |
|---|---|
| Finish-to-start | Task 2 starts only when task 1 finishes |
| Start-to-start | Task 4 starts only when task 3 has started |
| Finish-to-finish | Task 6 finishes only when task 5 finishes |
| Start-to-finish | Generally bad practice, according to APM |

Links can carry a lag (a deliberate delay after the predecessor) or a lead (an overlap, starting before the predecessor completes). Finish-to-start is the generally acceptable practice; APM marks start-to-finish as one to avoid.

## Critical path analysis: a worked example
This is the arithmetic the exam can test. The example below is illustrative, using the standard method.

A seven-activity project:

| Activity | Duration (weeks) | Depends on |
|---|---|---|
| A. Survey site | 4 | Nothing |
| B. Design | 6 | A |
| C. Procure materials | 5 | A |
| D. Build frame | 7 | B |
| E. Order fittings | 3 | B |
| F. Install services | 4 | C, D |
| G. Inspect and hand over | 2 | E, F |

Step 1 is the forward pass. Earliest start (ES) = latest EF of all predecessors. Earliest finish (EF) = ES + duration.

Step 2 is the backward pass. Latest finish (LF) = earliest LS of all successors. Latest start (LS) = LF − duration.

Step 3 is float = LS − ES.

| Activity | Dur | ES | EF | LS | LF | Float | Critical? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | 4 | 0 | 4 | 0 | 4 | 0 | Yes |
| B | 6 | 4 | 10 | 4 | 10 | 0 | Yes |
| C | 5 | 4 | 9 | 12 | 17 | 8 | No |
| D | 7 | 10 | 17 | 10 | 17 | 0 | Yes |
| E | 3 | 10 | 13 | 18 | 21 | 8 | No |
| F | 4 | 17 | 21 | 17 | 21 | 0 | Yes |
| G | 2 | 21 | 23 | 21 | 23 | 0 | Yes |

Critical path: A → B → D → F → G. Project duration: 23 weeks.

Check it by enumerating every path, because the critical path must be the longest:

| Path | Length |
|---|---|
| A → B → D → F → G | 23 |
| A → B → E → G | 15 |
| A → C → F → G | 15 |

23 − 15 = 8, which matches the float on C and E exactly. If your float figures do not reconcile with your path lengths, one of them is wrong.

Here is what float means in practice. Activity C can start up to 8 weeks late, or take 8 weeks longer, without delaying the project. Activity D cannot slip by a single day. Zero float means critical.

## Critical path vs critical chain: the difference
| | Critical path | Critical chain |
|---|---|---|
| Emphasis | Activities | Resources |
| Resource constraints | Not considered | Considered, alongside dependencies |
| Estimates used | Three-point, usually the most likely | The most optimistic: the best case |
| Where safety time sits | Inside each activity estimate | Stripped out and pooled as a buffer at the end of the chain |
| What gets monitored | Start and end dates, EVA, CPI, SPI | Rate of buffer consumption |
| Monitoring frequency | Monthly may suit many projects | At least weekly, often daily |

Both have the same purpose: to enable analysis of the work, determine start and end dates, and use scarce resource efficiently.

### Why critical chain exists

It targets three specific behaviours that make estimates unreliable:

- switching between several activities at once
- beginning work the moment its earliest start arrives, then holding the time until it is done
- opening tasks that are not properly ready, to avoid the stop-start of waiting on information, materials or sign-off

Tasks then run past an estimate that never allowed for any of this.

### What critical chain requires

- Resources available when an activity is due to start, so the team and anyone else needing the same resource must be consulted and reach agreement.
- A culture accepting that best-case estimates may not be achieved. The buffer is the safety net for the whole project, not for each task.
- Focus. Once working on a task, resources concentrate solely on completing it to standard. Start and end dates stop being the thing watched; what matters is people moving through the work quickly and efficiently.

Where time matters most, there is evidence of unusually strong results: better on-time delivery, better quality, lower cost.

The buffers get signed off and locked into the deployment baseline, which is what makes their consumption measurable.

## Schedule drivers: what else shapes it
This is the specific point of 20b, and the syllabus names the factors:

| Factor | How it impacts the schedule |
|---|---|
| Business-as-usual activities | BAU staff are often the same people the project needs. Operational peaks, year-end, seasonal demand and BAU incidents all take resource away. Transition into use has to fit around operational readiness |
| Costs | Funding release may depend on stage gates or product release, so activity cannot start until the money is drawn down. Cost limits constrain how much resource can be applied to compress a path |
| Quality | QA and QC take time and consume resources that must be scheduled. Testing, inspection, independent witnessing and rework all sit on the timeline, and rework after a failed test changes the plan |
| Risks | Contingency is time as well as money. Risk responses are scheduled activities. A materialising risk consumes buffer or float |
| Scope | Every change to scope changes the work, so changes the network. Scope creep lengthens paths silently if it is not controlled |

Both approaches require input from technical and BAU stakeholders, because they are the ones who know what will hit the schedule in time or resource terms. That is APM's own instruction, and it is the direct answer to 20b: you cannot build a credible schedule from inside the project alone.

Interfaces cut both ways. LO17 required understanding where the project touches other work in a programme or portfolio, and where it touches BAU, to avoid duplication, conflicts or omission.

core_content.body_markdown:
## Re-estimating: why do it at all
A schedule is never fixed. It gets reviewed continually, so that delivery still lands inside the time the project agreed to.

The underlying reason comes from LO19: estimating is not something done once for the business case and then closed. It runs continuously, sharpening as information arrives. The further the project goes, the more accurate its estimates get, and the better the decisions stakeholders can make on them.

So re-estimating is not an admission that the first plan was wrong. It is the plan doing what it was designed to do.

## Re-estimating: the triggers
| Trigger | Why the estimate changes |
|---|---|
| New information emerges | Early estimates were made with least knowledge. Detail replaces assumption |
| Actual performance data arrives | Real durations and costs from completed work are better predictors than forecasts |
| Scope changes | Approved changes alter the work, so alter the estimate |
| Risks materialise or close | A risk that occurs consumes contingency; one that passes releases it |
| Resource availability shifts | People leave, arrive, or get pulled into BAU |
| Dependencies change | A removed soft dependency shortens a path; a discovered one lengthens it |
| Rolling wave moves forward | The next wave of near-term work gets planned in detail for the first time |
| An iteration completes | Burndown data shows how efficiently the team worked, which sharpens the next estimate |

That last row is worth noting: in iterative working, re-estimating is built into the rhythm. Each iteration produces velocity data that improves the next forecast.

## Re-estimating: the benefits
- Better-informed decisions for stakeholders, because the forecast reflects what is now known.
- Earlier warning. A revised forecast surfaces a problem while there is still time to respond.
- Credibility. A schedule maintained honestly is trusted; one defended past the point of plausibility is not.
- Improved future estimating. Comparing estimate to actual is how estimating capability improves, which is the LO6 lessons-learned link.
- Contingency managed deliberately rather than consumed silently.

And the governance route: revised estimates go through change control, which is what then adjusts the integrated plan. Re-estimating does not mean quietly rewriting the baseline.

## Schedule optimisation: meeting a constraint
Optimisation means reshaping the schedule to meet a constraint, usually time and sometimes resource.

| Technique | What it does | What it costs |
|---|---|---|
| Reduce preferential or resource dependencies | Removes an artificial constraint, shortening a path | Requires accepting the governance or quality reason the dependency existed for |
| Apply more resource to critical activities | Shortens critical path duration | Costs money, and not all work divides |
| Overlap activities using leads | Starts a successor before its predecessor finishes | Increases risk of rework if the predecessor changes |
| Re-sequence the network | Finds a shorter arrangement of the same work | Needs the dependency logic re-agreed with experts |
| Level or smooth resources | Resolves resource conflicts (LO21) | Levelling may extend the end date; smoothing works within float |
| Reduce scope | Removes work from the network entirely | Requires change control, and may cost benefits |

Where to apply effort: the critical path. Compressing a non-critical activity achieves nothing, because it only increases that activity's float. This is the most common practical error, and a good scenario answer names it.

And a caution: compress a critical path far enough and a previously non-critical path becomes critical. In the worked example, driving A → B → D → F → G below 15 weeks would make both other paths critical, and further compression would need work on all three.

In iterative life cycles, optimisation works differently. The time and the money are what stay fixed, while scope and quality flex, so you agree a timebox and get through as much of the work as you efficiently can inside it. It may take a number of iterations before the output is genuinely fit for purpose. You do not compress the timebox; you change what goes in it.

## Progress monitoring: what tells you to re-estimate
Progress monitoring. The three elements required for performance measurement:

1. something to measure against: the baseline
2. what actually happened: real performance data
3. a judgement on what that performance means for the rest of the project

All three are needed. Data without a baseline is a number with nothing to compare it to; both without an assessment is reporting rather than control.

What gets monitored:

| Area | Includes |
|---|---|
| Progress | Whether planned scope is being delivered to the required quality; what has been committed and how cash is flowing; how contractors are performing |
| Opportunities and risks | Shifts in the project's environment; a changing risk profile and what it does to time buffers or cost contingency; opportunities spotted, and their effect |
| Health of the project | Stakeholder sentiment and engagement effectiveness; motivation and satisfaction of team members; health of supply chain relationships |

That third category is easily dismissed and shouldn't be. The project manager and team are responsible for monitoring the non-quantifiable areas of stakeholder engagement and team morale, while the people doing the work are best placed to track it, though plenty of organisations hand it to the PMO.

Frequency depends on circumstances and may change through the life cycle. With EVA or CPI, monthly may be appropriate for many projects, though critical activities may warrant more frequent tracking. Under critical chain the data comes in and gets reviewed weekly at minimum, frequently every day.

How to report it: typically quantitatively, with traffic-light approaches flagging areas in or out of control, individually or in a dashboard. But any project of real length needs its performance shown graphically, so a trend becomes visible and problems surface early. A trend is visible long before a threshold is breached. Iterative approaches use burndown charts.

And when recovery is not possible: when monitoring surfaces something the project cannot recover from, you replan and establish an amended baseline. That is the honest end point: not optimisation, but a new baseline through governance.

key_definitions.plain_english: Working out when everything happens, and keeping that answer current as things move.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The process of developing and maintaining schedules, identifying when activities are planned to be performed, considering dependencies, for internal and external resources and activities.

key_definitions.plain_english: The longest chain of dependent activities. Its length is the project's shortest possible duration.
key_definitions.apm_definition: A scheduling approach placing emphasis on activities. It identifies the series of tasks that must be completed promptly to ensure the project's timely and successful completion. It does not consider resource constraints.

key_definitions.plain_english: Critical path with the resource problem taken seriously, and safety time pooled into a buffer at the end.
key_definitions.apm_definition: A scheduling approach placing emphasis on resources, considering both task dependencies and external factors such as resource constraints, ensuring limited resource is considered in constructing a realistic schedule.

key_definitions.plain_english: How long an activity can slip without delaying the project. Zero float means it is on the critical path.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The flexibility identified when activities are planned using critical path analysis, indicating whether an activity is time critical or whether there is flexibility in the start date.

key_definitions.plain_english: The map of what depends on what, drawn before any dates are calculated.
key_definitions.apm_definition: A network diagram created by establishing the logic between activities, enabling estimates of duration based on effort to be made and used in a critical path analysis.

key_definitions.plain_english: Contingency pooled at the end rather than hidden inside every task. Shared, so it goes further.
key_definitions.apm_definition: In critical chain, the safety time stripped out of individual activity estimates and held at the end of a chain of activities, monitored by rate of consumption.

key_definitions.plain_english: Fixed time and cost, flexible scope and quality. The opposite of estimating how long something will take.
key_definitions.apm_definition: In an iterative life cycle, a fixed period with determined resources agreed in advance, within which work to fulfil the scope is completed as efficiently as possible.

key_definitions.plain_english: Plan the near future precisely and the far future roughly, because you cannot know the far future yet.
key_definitions.apm_definition: An approach often used for linear projects in which near-term activities are considered in detail, with later stages of the project considered at a higher level.

key_definitions.plain_english: The schedule of schedules.
key_definitions.apm_definition: On large or complex projects, the schedule that combines, coordinates and tracks several subordinate schedules dealing with different aspects of the project.

key_definitions.plain_english: Work remaining, plotted downwards over time. Its slope tells you whether the iteration will finish.
key_definitions.apm_definition: A chart used in iterative approaches to track completion and measure progress, used to calculate the efficiency of the team and improve future estimates.

body.where_this_fits: The schedule is where every other plan gets tested against time. Scope from LO17 becomes activities, dependencies from LO19 become a network, resources from LO21 constrain it, and risk from LO23 buys contingency in it. The distinction the exam wants is critical path versus critical chain: one emphasises activities and ignores resource constraints, the other starts from resources. Learn to calculate float by hand, because it is the one piece of arithmetic in this LO that gets tested directly.
learning_outcomes: 20a) Know how to define scope in terms of outputs, outcomes and benefits (including use of product, work and cost breakdown structures).

20b) Understand there are links and dependencies between activities within a project and business-as-usual activities — for example business-as-usual activities, costs, quality, risks and scope can all impact the schedule for the project.
20c) Understand the reasons for and benefits of re-estimating, and schedule optimisation, throughout the project life cycle.
progress_checkpoint: I can explain what scope covers and name the four breakdown structures, saying what each defines and how PBS feeds WBS.
I can name the dependency types and link types, and say which link type APM marks as bad practice.
I can perform a forward pass, backward pass and float calculation on a small network, and identify the critical path.
I can check my float figures against path lengths to verify a critical path calculation.
I can compare critical path and critical chain on emphasis, estimates used, where safety time sits, and what gets monitored.
I can explain the behaviours critical chain targets and what it requires from the team and the culture.
I can explain how BAU activities, costs, quality, risks and scope each impact the schedule.
I can give reasons and benefits for re-estimating, name schedule optimisation techniques, and say why only critical path compression shortens a project.

core_content.body_markdown:
## Resource management: what it covers
Resource management is getting hold of the resources a project needs, internal and external, and putting them to work. Both halves matter.

Why it matters: get the processes and controls wrong and you invite schedule delay, weaker quality, higher cost and thinner benefits. All four of the things the project is judged on.

A resource is anything needed to complete a project, though the emphasis falls on people resources and how best to leverage their skills and experience.

## Resource requirements: when identification starts
Identification normally starts once the high-level scope exists, because scope is what makes the work to be done visible. You cannot say who you need before you know what is being built, which is why LO17 comes first.

No two projects are the same. Scope, requirements and stakeholder needs all differ, so the particular skills, experience and competences each project needs differ with them.

## Resource requirements: the four things to identify
| Requirement | Detail |
|---|---|
| Skills | Hard skills, coding languages for example, and soft skills such as communication |
| Seniority | Junior, mid-level or senior, matched to the project's demands and complexity |
| Domain expertise | Whether previous experience in a particular sector is needed: financial services, construction |
| Qualifications | Whether industry-specific qualifications are required, such as CEng or ChPP |

Three routes work them out. Ask subject-matter experts. Look at what comparable projects resourced and what they learned. Or run a skills analysis such as job role mapping.

That middle route is the LO6 link: lessons learned from a comparable project is the cheapest source of a realistic resource profile.

## Capacity: estimating what is required
Once skills and competences are established, estimate the capacity required from each resource:

- full-time or part-time requirement
- how much effort, in hours or days each week

Past data and expert judgement both help here, together with top-down and bottom-up estimating used in combination. Those are the LO19 methods applied to people rather than money.

## Constraints: what shapes the answer
As the picture sharpens, weigh what cost, time and quality will each permit. The factors named:

| Factor | Effect |
|---|---|
| Resource availability | What actually exists to be had |
| Budget | What can be afforded |
| Seniority | Senior people cost more and are scarcer |
| Hiring lead times | How long it takes to get someone who is not already there |
| Location | A key consideration in a hybrid working world |

Together they settle whether the resource comes from inside or is brought in. That is the make-or-buy question from LO5, applied to people.

## Resource timing: how the life cycle changes it
A specific and examinable point:

| Life cycle | Resource profile |
|---|---|
| Linear | Design and planning specialisms tend to be concentrated at the front |
| Iterative | A similar project may require those skills throughout the entire life cycle |

Same project, same skills, entirely different demand curve.

## HR: working with the experts
Work with human resources experts to understand how resource requirements align with established job roles in the organisation. This standardises resource profiles and gives a foundation for the rest of capacity planning.

## Availability: the wider picture

Resource capacity planning is typically managed at programme, portfolio or organisational level and runs in three parts:

1. Identifying resource requirements, per project
2. Assessing total capacity, setting demand against capacity across programmes and portfolios
3. Capacity optimisation, squeezing the most benefit out of what exists

And the honest constraint: demand sometimes exceeds capacity, and something has to give. What you do then is lay out clearly what each initiative is worth, how it ranks and what it depends on, so stakeholders can choose between them on the facts.

Get resource requests in early, because late ones cost you time, and go to the resource managers to start the allocation conversation.

core_content.body_markdown:
## The RAM: its two inputs
| Structure | What it defines |
|---|---|
| OBS, the organisation breakdown structure | The people. Created by the choice of organisational structure, visualising the project hierarchy |
| WBS, the work breakdown structure | The work. Scope broken down into work packages representing the lowest level of work you intend to manage |

The OBS comes from the structural decision. Choosing functional, matrix or project (LO2) creates the project's organisational breakdown structure, which then enables the identification of resource requirements.

The WBS needs enough granularity. By the end of the breakdown, every item needs to be defined finely enough that it can be estimated and put on a schedule. Too coarse and you cannot allocate; too fine and you are managing minutiae.

## WBS plus OBS: combining them
Put the WBS and the OBS together and you get a responsibility assignment matrix. Work down one axis, people across the other.

What it shows: each separate item of work, who has been put on it, and what part they play.

## RACI coding: showing roles
The roles are shown using RACI coding:

| Letter | Role | Definition |
|---|---|---|
| R | Responsible | Conducting each piece of work |
| A | Accountable | Owns it, and signs it off once done |
| C | Consulted | Brought into the decisions, and supports the work along the way |
| I | Informed | About the work's progress |

The distinction that carries the marks: R does it, A owns it and signs it off. They can be the same person, but the accountability does not move even when the work is delegated. That is the same principle as sponsor and project manager in LO2, applied at task level.

One accountable per work item. Two people accountable for the same thing means nobody is.

## The RAM: what it is actually for
Three uses, all named by APM:

1. Allocating resources at the correct times, in line with the project's schedule.
2. Setting resources' expectations of what is required of them.
3. Tying each person and their piece of work back to what the project is for. That is the LO12 motivation point: people work better when they can see why their piece matters.

## The RAM: it is not fixed
Structure and allocation both shift as the project moves and new information lands. So continue to regularly engage with resource managers to ensure new or updated allocations are agreed and actioned, a process that starts during resource identification and does not stop there.

And where a change to resource requirements is needed, weigh what it does to things like quality and cost, then put a formal change request against the baseline through the organisation's change control process, so that change requests and impact assessments are reviewed with proper transparency and control (LO24).

core_content.body_markdown:
## Resource categories: how resources are grouped
Pulling the categorisations together:

| Basis | Categories |
|---|---|
| Type | Labour, your own people or contracted in; services bought in, such as development work or legal advice; materials and consumables, whether finished or raw; assets like equipment, vehicles and infrastructure, purchased, leased or rented |
| Skills | Hard skills and soft skills |
| Seniority | Junior, mid-level, senior |
| Domain and qualification | Sector expertise; industry-specific qualifications |
| Source | Internal or external |
| Commitment | Full-time or part-time, estimated in hours or days per week |

A scheduling consequence worth knowing: some organisations put every resource into the schedule, materials and procurement phasing included, while others schedule labour alone, with non-labour costs appearing only in the budget (LO22). Both are legitimate.

## Linear schedules: allocating resources
1. Define the work through the WBS into work packages.
2. Pin down as precisely as you can the start and end of every work package.
3. Build the RAM and use it to allocate resources at the correct times, in line with the schedule.
4. Request allocation from resource managers, as early as possible.

The demand profile is front-loaded for specialisms, with design and planning skills concentrated early. Resource conflicts are resolved by levelling or smoothing (21d) before the deployment baseline is set.

Because the plan is fixed at approval, a change in resource requirement is a change to the baseline and goes through change control.

## Iterative schedules: allocating resources
Iterative projects commit resources over limited periods called timeboxes. Within a timebox, a fixed period with determined resources is agreed, and the work is completed as efficiently as possible.

| | Linear | Iterative |
|---|---|---|
| Commitment horizon | The whole plan, fixed at approval | One timebox at a time |
| Skill demand curve | Front-loaded design and planning specialisms | Those skills needed throughout the entire life cycle |
| What flexes | Time and cost flex against fixed scope and quality | Time and cost are fixed; scope and quality flex |
| Team shape | Specialists arrive and leave as their phase runs | Stable cross-functional team held across iterations |
| Adjusting resource | Change request against the baseline | Adjust what enters the next timebox |

The practical consequence: an iterative project needs its capabilities available continuously, so a specialist who can only be released for four weeks is a genuine constraint on the approach, not merely a scheduling inconvenience.

## Managing resources: once allocated
Resources directly contribute to the deliverables, so they need managing closely. Four common monitoring methods:

| Method | What it tells you |
|---|---|
| Timesheets | How many hours each person actually put into project work |
| Monitoring tasks | Whether work is completed on time and to quality |
| Stakeholder feedback | How the resource is actually performing |
| Resource histogram or demand profile | Utilisation, visualised |

Data gets collated into a resource management report, setting performance, availability and utilisation against what the project expected.

## Resource governance: set it up early
Establish it as early as possible, so there is a route to report progress, raise issues, and keep expectations aligned with the resource managers. It should:

- report how resources are performing, with escalation routes and fallback plans ready for underperformance
- monitor constraints affecting resource availability, feeding into organisational capacity planning and risk management
- track resource utilisation, giving transparency on actual utilisation against the project's forecast

And the standing reality: you are permanently in competition with other projects and programmes for the same people. That is why levelling and smoothing exist. They are what you do when constraints cannot be overcome.

activities.title: Levelling or smoothing?
activities.heading: Levelling and smoothing: the two techniques

core_content.body_markdown:
## Levelling and smoothing: the two techniques
Both are ways of making project-level resource capacity go further once the constraint itself cannot be shifted. They are the two most common examples.

The cleanest way to hold them is by the question each one answers. APM frames them exactly this way, and the questions are more reliable than any rule of thumb.

| | Resource levelling | Resource smoothing |
|---|---|---|
| The question it answers | Given the people we actually have, when does this finish? | To hit what we promised, what resource do we need? |
| What is held fixed | Resource constraints | Scope, quality and time |
| What is allowed to move | The timeline | Cost |
| Use when | You cannot get more resource | The date cannot move |

Levelling holds resources fixed, so the end date flexes. You work out what the available people can actually deliver and when that finishes.

Smoothing holds the date fixed, so cost flexes. You work out what resource is needed to hit the commitments and accept the bill.

A memory hook worth carrying: levelling moves the level of the finish line; smoothing smooths the peaks and troughs and pays for it.

## Levelling and smoothing: what each involves
Levelling leans on critical path or critical chain to rework the tasks and the schedule, wringing the most out of whoever is available right now. It is scheduling beneath a resource ceiling.

Smoothing is more than adding people. It is not simply a matter of hiring more people: it also means finding ways to get more out of existing capacity, or rearranging work so the peaks and troughs flatten.

That second half is the more interesting one for a scenario answer. Reshaping *when* work happens, so demand sits flatter across the same period, is smoothing without buying anything.

## Resource optimisation: the output
What project-level optimisation produces is a curve: how resource, and so how spend, is planned to be deployed over time to finish the scope at the quality required.

That curve is what feeds LO22, because costing works from the resourced schedule. Levelling and smoothing happen before the budget is finalised, not after.

## Optimisation above project level: how it differs
At programme, portfolio or organisational level, optimisation works differently:

- resequencing or phasing initiatives so their resource demands stop colliding
- identifying synergies between initiatives
- project and programme phasing, handled more strategically

So a resource conflict a project cannot solve internally may be solvable by the portfolio deciding which initiative goes first. That is the escalation route, and it connects to LO2, because the decision sits above the project's authority.

## When neither works: the trade-off
Demand outstrips capacity sometimes, and a trade-off becomes unavoidable. The answer is not more optimisation: it is setting out plainly what each initiative is worth, where it ranks and what it depends on, so stakeholders can make the priority call on the facts.

And where the project's own resource requirement must change, work out what that does to quality and cost, then take a formal change request to the baseline through change control.
core_content.outcome_title: Resource levelling and resource smoothing

worked_examples.answer: Smooth. The date cannot move, so cost is the thing you let flex: contract the extra five, or reshape February's work until the peak flattens. Levelling would answer a question nobody asked, because it moves the finish date you have no permission to move.

key_definitions.plain_english: Getting hold of what the project needs, mostly people, and putting it where the work is.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The acquisition and deployment of the internal and external resources required to deliver the project, programme or portfolio.

key_definitions.plain_english: Anything the work consumes. In practice, usually people.
key_definitions.apm_definition: Anything that is needed to complete a project, though the emphasis falls on people resources and how best to leverage their skills and experience.

key_definitions.plain_english: Work down one axis, people across the other, roles in the cells. The grid that stops 'I thought you were doing that'.

key_definitions.plain_english: Resources are what they are, so the end date moves to fit them.

key_definitions.plain_english: The date holds, so you find the resource to make it happen, and pay for it.
key_definitions.apm_definition: A technique that ensures scope, quality and time are achieved while accepting an impact on cost, answering the question: what resources are required to deliver the expectations?

key_definitions.plain_english: A bar chart of demand over time. Peaks and troughs are what levelling and smoothing attack.
key_definitions.apm_definition: A visualisation of resource utilisation over time, used to show performance, availability and utilisation against the project's expectations.

key_definitions.plain_english: Working out what all the projects need against what the organisation actually has.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The process, typically managed at programme, portfolio or organisational level, of establishing resource requirements, assessing total capacity, and optimising capacity to create maximum benefit.

key_definitions.plain_english: How much of someone's time the project is really getting, against how much it planned for.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The proportion of a resource's available capacity actually used on project work, tracked to provide transparency on actual utilisation against the project's forecast.

body.where_this_fits: Resources are the constraint the schedule collides with. LO20's critical path deliberately ignores them; critical chain and this LO are what put them back. The distinction the exam tests hardest is levelling versus smoothing, and APM frames it slightly differently from the way it is commonly taught elsewhere, so learn APM's two questions rather than a half-remembered rule of thumb.

21d) Know the differences between resource smoothing and resource levelling.

core_content.body_markdown:
## Budgeting and cost control: where budgeting sits
Budgeting and cost control has four elements:

1. estimating what it will cost
2. agreeing a budget
3. tracking actual and forecast spend against that budget
4. shutting the finances down properly at the end

The first two are 22a; the third is 22b; the fourth closes the LO.

Cost planning runs alongside resource planning and scheduling, and takes the resource-optimised schedule as one of its inputs. That ordering matters and is worth stating in an answer: you cannot cost a schedule you have not built, or a resource plan you have not levelled.

## The cost breakdown structure: scope in budget terms
The CBS defines scope in terms of the project budget, and it is the fourth of the breakdown structures you met in LO17 and LO20.

| Structure | Defines |
|---|---|
| PBS | The things to create |
| WBS | The activities to complete |
| OBS | The allocation of people |
| CBS | The project budget |

Building the budget through a CBS means every cost traces to a work package and a deliverable. That is what makes variance analysis possible later, because an overspend can be located rather than only observed.

## Cost types: the ones to know
All types of cost get considered:

| Category | Covers |
|---|---|
| Labour | People, both internal and contracted |
| Services | Software development, legal advice |
| Materials and consumables | Both finished and raw materials |
| Assets | Equipment, vehicles and infrastructure, bought, leased or rented |

## Cost behaviour: the distinctions to know
Then there are the behavioural distinctions the syllabus names:

| Pair | Distinction |
|---|---|
| Fixed vs variable | A fixed cost is unaffected by scale or quantity; a variable cost moves with how much you use or make |
| One-off vs recurring | Pay it once, like buying a computer, or pay it again and again, like a software licence renewal |
| Capital vs revenue | How each is treated follows the organisation's accounting rules, and capital spend is tightly controlled, especially in the public sector |
| Direct vs indirect | Direct costs attach to a specific work package or deliverable; indirect costs support the project without tracing to one item |

The fixed and variable distinction behaves differently in an iterative life cycle. In linear work, fixed cost sits as a baseline with variable cost rising by quantity. In iterative work, each iteration carries its own fixed cost, and total cost rises in steps by released scope rather than smoothly by units made. That is why a client or sponsor can cap future commitment by cutting how many iterations are funded, each one being a discrete, largely fixed cost.

## Cost profiling: not only totalling
Beyond totalling the budget, costs get profiled across the initiative's life, and that profile is a cash flow forecast. In earned value terms it is the budgeted cost of work scheduled (BCWS), which is the same thing as planned value.

So the budget is not a number, it is a curve. That curve becomes the baseline everything in 22b is measured against.

Timing of funding release matters too: money may only be released once products ship, certification passes, or a stage gate clears. On iterative work, funding release is often tied to iterations. A budget that exists but cannot be drawn down yet is not available money.

## Cost estimating: approaches by cost type
Approaches differ by cost type. Material costs come off published prices, multiplied by estimated volumes. Subcontractors on time and materials need an estimate of the hours they will work. On fixed price, the supplier estimates the time and includes contingency or a risk premium, which is the LO5 link: fixed price transfers risk, and the supplier prices it in.

The bias to watch is optimism bias. It is the most prominent one, the tendency to assume everything will run the ideal course. Two counters:

- review and challenge processes
- contingency for each cost area

## Whole-life costing: the full cost of ownership
Sustainability is important in project-based working, and whole-life costing is one way to ensure long-term impacts are considered. Increasingly, budgets are planned to the end-of-life and decommissioning stages.

This is the LO3 link made financial. The cheapest option to build is frequently not the cheapest to own, and LO5's lifetime cost of ownership makes the same argument in procurement.

## Contingency and management reserve: planning for the unknown
There is no magic purse with unlimited funds, so experienced professionals ensure budgets include contingency and a management reserve.

| Type | Covers | Released by |
|---|---|---|
| Planned contingency | Known risks and anticipated events | Authority to draw down, once the risk occurs |
| Management or project reserve | Unanticipated issues | The governance board |

It is not a secret stash that makes problems disappear. It is a management tool, and governance controls it.

Contingency can appear as line items in a budget, as additional timeboxed iterations, or as a management reserve held across the whole project.

Different levels of the organisation can hold contingency for different kinds of risk. Handing the whole lot to the project professional takes real trust from sponsor and board, because they need confidence it will only be spent where genuinely needed. Things like currency or interest rate exposure sit better at organisational level.

## Governance: it sits over all of it
Every pound spent falls under governance oversight and decision-making, which puts cost planning right at the centre of governance, so how much detail and rigour is applied depends on the organisation. It depends as well on how risky and how large the initiative is, and on which workstream or phase you are in. Iterative life cycles can control expenditure more easily, so they can tolerate reduced rigour at the outset.

core_content.body_markdown:
## Cost control: what it does
The budget is set and the expenditure scheduled, delivery starts and the money goes out. Managing what actually gets spent against what was budgeted is cost control.

The baseline is that same cash flow forecast the project was approved on. Monitoring happens against that and against the approved budget.

How often to monitor: track spend as close to real time as you can manage, and the quicker money is going out, the more often you should be looking. That is a useful rule because it is specific.

Project systems can hook into enterprise accounting software and report expenditure in real time, but even those run behind whatever the project has already committed to. Committed is not the same as recorded, and holding an accurate, current picture of budget status is hard, which is why big projects bring in dedicated finance and cost management specialists.

## Monitoring: why it matters
| Reason | What it enables |
|---|---|
| The primary reason | So that a deviation from plan can be corrected quickly |
| Recovery or re-forecast | If expenditure will exceed budget, the team investigates and intervenes. Where the original budget cannot be recovered, a revised expenditure forecast gets produced, and that may need signing off by a client, sponsor or governance structure |
| Authorising payment | Knowing when contractors have met their obligations, so payments can be authorised, subject to any outstanding quality control |
| Supporting stage gates | Often what unlocks the next tranche of budget |
| Contingency drawdown | Where overspends cannot be recovered, seeking authority to draw down budgeted contingency, or in extreme cases additional, unbudgeted funding |

## Financial reports: what they contain
Good governance needs good information. Reports combine three things:

1. where things stand now, and which way they are trending
2. a look backwards at why the plan was missed
3. a look forwards: the forecast, and what will be done about it

All three. A report with status but no reasons cannot be acted on; one with no forecast tells the board nothing about where this ends.

Who wants them: the sponsor, project board, PMO or corporate finance function, and stakeholders beyond the sponsoring organisation, including lenders, investors, grant-giving bodies or shareholders. They want to know the money they lent, invested or gave is being used wisely. For substantial programmes, financial reports may appear in statutory reporting and annual reports.

## Earned value: the problem it solves
Earned value analysis solves a specific problem. Comparing budget to actual spend tells you how much you spent, but not what you got for it, so a project that has spent half its budget might be half built or barely started. Earned value adds the third measure that makes the comparison meaningful.

## Earned value: the four base measures
| Measure | Also called | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| PV, planned value | BCWS, budgeted cost of work scheduled | What the work planned for this point was budgeted to cost |
| EV, earned value | BCWP, budgeted cost of work performed | What the work actually completed was budgeted to cost |
| AC, actual cost | ACWP, actual cost of work performed | What has actually been spent |
| BAC, budget at completion | | The total approved budget |

The trick to remembering BCWS and BCWP: both are *budgeted* costs. Scheduled is what you planned to have done, performed is what you have done. Only ACWP is a real-money figure.

## Earned value: the derived measures
| Measure | Formula | Reads as |
|---|---|---|
| CV, cost variance | EV − AC | Negative = over budget |
| SV, schedule variance | EV − PV | Negative = behind schedule |
| CPI, cost performance index | EV ÷ AC | Below 1.0 = over budget |
| SPI, schedule performance index | EV ÷ PV | Below 1.0 = behind schedule |
| EAC, estimate at completion | BAC ÷ CPI | Forecast final cost if current efficiency continues |

Both variances subtract from EV. Both indices divide EV. Get that and the formulas stop needing memorisation, because the only thing that changes is whether you compare against actual cost, which is money, or against planned value, which is progress.

## Earned value: a worked example
Take a project with a budget at completion of £240,000, reviewed at the end of month 6:

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| PV (BCWS), work scheduled by now | £120,000 |
| EV (BCWP), work actually completed | £96,000 |
| AC (ACWP), actually spent | £128,000 |

Cost variance: CV = EV − AC = £96,000 − £128,000 = −£32,000. Negative, so over budget.

Schedule variance: SV = EV − PV = £96,000 − £120,000 = −£24,000. Negative, so behind schedule.

Cost performance index: CPI = EV ÷ AC = 96,000 ÷ 128,000 = 0.75. For every £1 spent, 75p of budgeted value has been earned.

Schedule performance index: SPI = EV ÷ PV = 96,000 ÷ 120,000 = 0.80. The project is earning value at 80% of the planned rate.

Estimate at completion: EAC = BAC ÷ CPI = £240,000 ÷ 0.75 = £320,000.

Forecast overspend: £320,000 − £240,000 = £80,000, a third over budget, if current cost efficiency continues.

Reading it in one sentence: the project has completed less work than planned and spent more than that work was worth, so it is both behind and over, and on current performance it will finish about a third above budget.

## Earned value analysis: what it gives you
CPI shows how efficiently money is being turned into value, and SPI shows how productively work is being completed. Between them they let schedule and budget performance be judged side by side, which no other technique in the course does.

The exception worth knowing: none of this applies under critical chain, which watches rate of buffer consumption instead, buffer used against chain completed. Where a customer insists on the earned value figures, they can be generated from an unbuffered version of the schedule.

## Iterative life cycles: easier to control
Monitoring and controlling an iterative project is usually easier, because most of what an iteration costs is fixed, and future commitment can be capped by funding fewer iterations.

However, an iterative approach is often chosen when there is high uncertainty about the specification or the development process, which makes the funding requirement hard to judge at the start. That is the honest counterweight from the financial reporting section, and it makes forecasting difficult, unless the project runs to a fixed total budget.

Essentially, iterative work is easier to control and harder to forecast. Both are true, and an answer that says only one of them is half an answer.

## Financial closedown: the forgotten element
The fourth element, and the one people forget:

| Task | What it involves |
|---|---|
| Meet outstanding commitments | Invoices from contractors, consultants and suppliers all get processed and paid. A contract is not complete until every bill against it has been settled |
| Secure transition funding | Where budgets include transition activities, secure drawdown of those funds |
| Return contingency | Professionals aim not to draw down all contingency or management reserves. These may be returned to the organisation, or held as reserves for other initiatives within a portfolio or programme |
| Close out timesheets and expenses | The last costs to surface are usually unsubmitted timesheets and expense claims, so put a deadline on them |
| Assess financial performance | Compare actual expenditure against the business case budget, with a final financial report |
| Close cost centres and archive | Close project-specific cost centres, review team access to finance systems, and secure and archive financial records per organisational policy, so they are available for any potential future audit |

That last row connects to LO6 and LO15: records are retained because someone may need to audit them, and retention is governed by policy and legislation.

key_definitions.apm_definition: Estimating costs, establishing a budget, and considering how and when funding will be drawn down and committed. The resource-optimised schedule is an input to it.

key_definitions.plain_english: Watching what actually gets spent against what was agreed, and acting when they diverge.
key_definitions.apm_definition: Managing actual costs against the budget during delivery: forecasting costs, monitoring spending, controlling variances and reporting on status.

key_definitions.plain_english: The budget broken down the same way the work is, so spend can be traced to what produced it.
key_definitions.apm_definition: A breakdown structure defining scope in terms of the project budget, decomposing cost by work package and deliverable.

key_definitions.plain_english: Fixed costs are there whether you build one or a thousand. Variable costs rise with volume.
key_definitions.apm_definition: Fixed costs do not depend on scale or quantities. Variable costs change with use or quantity.

key_definitions.plain_english: Direct is what this task cost. Indirect is the overhead that keeps everything running.
key_definitions.apm_definition: Direct costs are attributable to a specific work package or deliverable. Indirect costs support the project without being traceable to one item of work.

key_definitions.plain_english: Costing the whole life, not only the build. This is the sustainability link: the cheapest thing to build is often not the cheapest to own.
key_definitions.apm_definition: Planning budgets to the end-of-life and decommissioning stages of an initiative, ensuring the long-term impacts are considered.

key_definitions.plain_english: Assuming things go well. Systematic, predictable, and the reason estimates need challenging.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The most prominent estimating bias, leading to overconfidence that events will follow an ideal course. Countered by review and challenge processes, and by including contingency for each cost area.

key_definitions.plain_english: Money held for the risks you identified. Drawn down with authority when one occurs.
key_definitions.apm_definition: Resource set aside to manage known risks and anticipated events.

key_definitions.plain_english: Money held for what you did not see coming. Released by the governance board, not the project manager.
key_definitions.apm_definition: Extra funds available to deal with unanticipated issues, held across the whole project. Also called project reserve.

key_definitions.plain_english: What the work you have finished was supposed to cost. The measure that makes progress and spend comparable.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The budgeted cost of work performed, meaning the value of work actually completed, measured at budgeted rates.

key_definitions.plain_english: How much value you get per pound spent. Below 1.0 means over budget.
key_definitions.apm_definition: A measure of the efficiency of spend, calculated as earned value divided by actual cost.

key_definitions.plain_english: How fast you are earning value against plan. Below 1.0 means behind schedule.
key_definitions.apm_definition: A measure of productivity, calculated as earned value divided by planned value.

body.where_this_fits: The money half of the delivery controls, and the twin of LO20's schedule. Earned value is the technique that joins them. Learn the four base measures and the four derived ones, and be able to interpret a CPI or SPI figure in a sentence.

core_content.body_markdown:
## Risk vs issue management: the two disciplines
| | Risk management | Issue management |
|---|---|---|
| What it handles | Uncertainty that has not happened yet: threats and opportunities | Something that has happened and exceeded tolerance |
| Process | Identify, assess and respond appropriately | React appropriately, including escalation to the relevant authority |
| Who resolves it | Risk owner, within the plan | Requires support from the sponsor to agree a resolution |

One definition decides which process applies: an issue arises the moment delegated work breaches its tolerances, or is certain to.

Issues are different to problems, and that is the distinction most people miss. A problem is dealt with day to day by the project manager and the team. An issue needs the sponsor. The dividing line is tolerance, not severity or inconvenience.

They are related but not the same.

- A risk, or a cluster of them, materialising is often what produces an issue.
- An issue running now can itself generate fresh risks, and can force you to re-score how likely and how damaging risks you had already logged now look.

So a materialised risk becomes an issue, and that issue seeds new risks. The two registers talk to each other.

## Risk and issue management: the benefits
Direct answer to 23a:

| Benefit | How it arises |
|---|---|
| Minimises the effects of uncertainty | The core purpose. All projects bring change and therefore uncertainty |
| A more robust deployment baseline and PMP | Stated directly as the result |
| Confidence to stakeholders | They can see risk is being got ahead of rather than reacted to |
| Protects organisational reputation | Named explicitly |
| Realistic plans and appropriate contingency | Analysis sizes the contingency rather than guessing it |
| Prioritisation | It is unrealistic to believe every risk can be managed, so prioritisation lets the top risks be addressed |
| Better escalation | Analysis reveals which risks warrant the sponsor's or the board's attention |
| Opportunities captured | Uncertainty sometimes helps you hit your objectives rather than hindering |
| Decisions at the right level | Issue management keeps people inside the authority they were given, and puts each resolution decision at the level that should be taking it |

That last one is the strongest argument for issue management specifically, and it links straight to LO2.

## A diagnostic: when issues keep arriving
Where issues keep arriving, the plans and the controls themselves are probably the problem. Repeated issues are a symptom rather than a run of bad luck: the tolerances, the plan or the controls are probably wrong.

A related bias sits underneath that. Project professionals understandably prioritise issues over risks, because issues are happening now whereas risks are only potential. Understandable, but it is how a project ends up permanently firefighting.

## Contingency: resource set aside for one purpose
Contingency planning means putting resource aside that exists for one purpose only: responding to risk and uncertainty. It bridges the gap that risk creates, covering:

- known risks
- unknown risks
- the uncertainty of early-project estimates

That third category is the one people forget: contingency covers estimating uncertainty as well as identified risk events.

Two types:

| Type | Covers | Released by |
|---|---|---|
| Planned contingency | Known risks and anticipated events | Authority to draw down when the risk occurs |
| Management or project reserve | Unanticipated issues | The governance board |

Contingency is time as well as money: buffers in the schedule as much as reserve in the budget. References to budget contingency apply equally to schedule contingency.

One framing matters more than any other. Contingency is not a secret stash that makes problems disappear. Governance controls it, as a management tool.

The drawdown route (LO22): risk previously identified goes to planned contingency. Not identified goes to management reserve, released by the board. Reserve insufficient means a change request for additional funding.

Analysis sizes it. Probabilistic analysis is what lets you settle how much contingency buys the confidence level you need, which is why no business case or plan is complete without risk analysis behind it.

core_content.body_markdown:
## Risk management: the process
| Stage | Purpose and why it matters |
|---|---|
| Identification | Surface every risk to the objectives that can be known about, using stakeholder expertise to do it. Describe each as cause, event and impact so opinions align and group bias is addressed. Assign a risk owner, the individual or group best placed to assess and manage it. Document in the risk register |
| Analysis | Assess probability and impact to prioritise. It is unrealistic to believe every risk can be managed, so this is what makes the top risks visible |
| Response | Decide and plan the response, proactive or reactive (23c). If investing time and money is justified, resources are planned and agreed and the deployment baseline and PMP updated |
| Monitoring | Keeping the risk conversation alive is crucial. The process captures and manages emerging risks; new knowledge is acted upon and contingency estimates refined |
| Escalation | Priority risks go up to the sponsor or the governance board, which is how expectations get managed and decisions get made on evidence |
| Closure | Close a risk once it has happened, or once it no longer can |

It cycles rather than concludes, because project work itself keeps moving. Not a stage you complete.

Closure is the stage most often skipped. A register full of risks that can no longer happen buries the ones that still can.

## Risk analysis: qualitative and quantitative
Two techniques:

| Technique | What it does | When |
|---|---|---|
| Qualitative | Ranks risk events on how likely they are and how hard they would hit schedule, cost, benefits and any other objective at stake | As a minimum, always. For many projects a qualitative approach is sufficient |
| Quantitative | Focuses on specific risk-based decisions using decision trees, sensitivity analysis, or a holistic view of overall project risk | For large or complex projects, and to support the investment decision |

Probabilistic analysis predicts the probability of a variety of outcomes, and Monte Carlo simulation is the example given. Its outputs help you:

- see how likely a given end date, final cost or benefit level actually is
- put odds on delivering the business case and the plan, and decide accordingly
- fix contingency at the level that buys the confidence required

Two points about people, not technique:

- Focus on the objectives that are at risk, then fine-tune project-specific impact scales. Generic scales produce generic prioritisation.
- What looks risky, and why, varies from person to person, so get a spread of project professionals into the analysis. Their different perspectives add value and integrity to the process.

## Issue management: the process
Wherever the issue came from, you run the same process:

| Stage | What happens |
|---|---|
| Log and analyse | Straight into the issue register, then analysed fast: what caused it, and what it costs if left |
| Escalate | To the sponsor, who may in turn escalate to the governance board for resolution |
| Assign actions | To whoever is genuinely best placed to own it |
| Apply change control | An issue can end up changing scope, and when it does the agreed change control process applies |
| Track to closure | Management is tracked from identification through to resolution |
| Update risk analysis | Because a current issue may cause new risks or change existing assessments |

Speed is part of the process. 'Analysis takes place quickly' is stated for issues and not for risks, because an unresolved issue is actively consuming the project.

## The two barriers: what stops it working
Simple enough as a concept, but two things reliably stop it working:

1. Reluctance to escalate issues early. That connects to LO12 and LO14, because a blame culture guarantees late escalation.
2. The governance board treating the symptom rather than addressing the root cause.

## Life cycle differences: how the stages vary
| | Linear | Iterative |
|---|---|---|
| Identification | Concentrated in the early stages, often through group workshops, feeding the initial risk register | Continuous, since each iteration surfaces risks as scope is drawn down |
| Analysis | Fuller up-front analysis supporting a business case approved once | Lighter, repeated. Detail arrives with the work |
| Response | Responses planned into the baseline; changing them means change control | Responses can be absorbed into the next iteration's plan |
| Monitoring | At defined review points and gates | At the end of every iteration, alongside the value-proposition test |
| Escalation | Through the governance structure at gates or by exception | More frequent and lower ceremony, but the same tolerance principle |
| Closure | At review points | Each iteration closes risks that can no longer occur |
| Contingency | Held as budget and schedule buffers | Can appear as additional timeboxed iterations |

The structural reason for the difference: an iterative project re-justifies itself every cycle, so risk review is built into the rhythm. A linear project reviews at gates, and between them the machinery is change control.

However, the principle holds either way. No business case and no plan, project or programme, whichever life cycle, is complete without risk analysis behind it. Iterative does not mean less rigorous. It means more often and closer to the work.
core_content.outcome_title: The risk and issue management processes, and how they differ by life cycle

core_content.body_markdown:
## Risk responses: the two modes
| Mode | Definition |
|---|---|
| Proactive | A planned and implemented response: we do something now |
| Reactive | The response gets worked out now and sits unused unless the risk happens |

The distinction is *when you act*, not how serious the risk is. A reactive response is still a planned response, and the plan sits waiting.

## Proactive responses: the six options
| | Threats | Opportunities |
|---|---|---|
| Change the scope | Avoid: change the scope to eliminate the cause | Exploit: change the scope to make sure the opportunity happens |
| Change probability or impact | Reduce how likely the threat is, how much it would hurt, or both | Enhance: push up how likely the opportunity is, how much it would gain, or both |
| Involve another party | Transfer the cost: insure against it, or hand it to someone better equipped to carry it | Share the benefit, possibly through a joint venture |

Learn them as three mirrored pairs, not six items. Avoid mirrors exploit; reduce mirrors enhance; transfer mirrors share. Each pair uses the same mechanism, pointed in opposite directions.

## Reactive responses: the two options
| Side | Response | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Threat | Accept | The threat is accepted with a contingent response, so you carry it with a plan ready |
| Opportunity | Reject | The opportunity may not be worthwhile pursuing |

Accept is not the same as ignore. It is a decision, recorded, usually with contingency behind it. Reject is not pessimism either. It is a judgement that chasing this opportunity costs more than it returns.

## Choosing a response: weighing the cost
Someone has to decide whether spending time and money up front to cut exposure is worth it, and how much exposure is tolerable is set by what the investors and wider stakeholders are willing to carry.

That is the deciding factor, and it is not the project manager's to set. LO1's risk appetite reappears here as the thing that determines how much response is warranted.

Where investing is justified:

- the resources it takes get planned and agreed
- the deployment baseline and the PMP both get updated

A risk response is scheduled, resourced work. It is not free, and it changes the plan.

## Perception: how it shapes response
People perceive risk in different ways. Plenty of factors shape how someone reads risk and what attitude they take to it: some conscious, some not, some purely emotional. So you have to talk to a spread of stakeholders to find out where each of them stands.

Without that engagement the responses you design will not be ones anybody adopts. You end up with responses that are technically correct and that nobody will implement.

## Opportunity management: the forgotten half of risk
The half of risk that gets forgotten. Uncertainty sometimes helps you hit your objectives, and that is risk's positive face.

Look for opportunities across the whole life cycle, and run them through exactly the process and tools you use on threats.

Same identification, same analysis, same register, same owner, same monitoring. The only thing that changes is the direction of the impact and which three responses apply.
