core_content.body_markdown:
## Tolerances: the mechanism
Get the tolerance levels agreed, or issue management has nothing to stand on.

That sentence carries the whole sub-outcome. Tolerance is what converts a judgement call into a rule: inside it, the project manager acts; outside it, someone else decides. It is LO2's delegated limits of authority, applied to uncertainty.

What escalation buys is stated directly. An issue goes up to people who:

- see the organisation more strategically than the project can
- can put more resource behind it if that is what it takes
- have the authority to change scope

They also hold the ultimate power: where an issue leaves the project unviable, it can be cancelled.

That is the strongest single reason governance matters here. No amount of project-level effort can cancel a project that should be cancelled.

## Governance: what it provides
| Governance function | Why risk and issue management needs it |
|---|---|
| Sets risk appetite | How much exposure is tolerable comes from what the investors and wider stakeholders will carry, not from the project |
| Sets tolerances | Defines the boundary between a problem and an issue |
| Receives escalation | Priority risks travel up to the sponsor or the governance board |
| Releases contingency | Planned contingency is drawn down with authority; management reserve is released by the governance board |
| Authorises scope change | Issues may result in changes to scope, so change control must be followed |
| Decides continuation | Including cancelling an initiative made unviable |
| Provides confidence | Stakeholders can see risk is being got ahead of rather than reacted to, which also protects the organisation's reputation |

Three things shape how risk management is set up: the organisation's appetite for risk, the governance already in place, and how big and complicated the change is. Governance is an explicit input to how risk management is designed, not only a recipient of its outputs.

## Decision levels: why issue management keeps them right
Issue management is a genuine project control. Run properly, it keeps people inside the authority they were given and puts each resolution decision at the level that should be taking it.

Both halves matter:

- Working within delegated authority means the project manager does not quietly absorb something they were not authorised to absorb.
- Decisions at the appropriate level means the sponsor or board is not asked to adjudicate on day-to-day problems either.

Escalating too little and escalating everything are both governance failures.

## Escalation: what governance enables
Escalating is what lets expectations be managed and decisions be taken on evidence. The words doing the work are *on evidence*, which is why analysis, the risk register and clear risk descriptions matter. A board asked to decide on an unanalysed risk is guessing.

And since no business case or plan is complete without risk analysis behind it, governance leans on it at approval as much as during delivery.

## Governance failures: the five to know
The five failures worth knowing by name:

| Failure | Consequence |
|---|---|
| Reluctance to escalate issues early | Problems arrive at the board too late to be solved cheaply |
| The board treating the symptom rather than the root cause | The same issue recurs |
| Tolerances not agreed | No basis for deciding what escalates, so escalation becomes personality-driven |
| Continual issues | May indicate an underlying problem with project plans and controls |
| Contingency treated as spare money | Undermines the control it was meant to provide |

## The governance triangle: the connection
From LO7: governance leans on assurance to make its decisions sound, risk analysis points assurance at the greatest vulnerabilities, and what assurance finds sharpens the risk picture. Weakness in any one compromises the others.

So risk management is not merely governed. It is one of the three legs holding governance up.

key_definitions.plain_english: Working out what might happen, how much it would matter, and what to do about it before it does.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The process that allows project professionals to identify, assess and respond appropriately to risks. It involves deciding which threats to actively minimise and which opportunities to maximise or pursue.

key_definitions.plain_english: Something that has gone beyond what the project manager was authorised to absorb. It needs the sponsor.
key_definitions.apm_definition: What occurs when the tolerances of delegated work have been exceeded, or when the tolerances will definitely be exceeded. Issues require support from the sponsor to agree a resolution.

key_definitions.plain_english: Something inside your tolerances. You just deal with it.
key_definitions.apm_definition: A day-to-day matter dealt with by the project manager and the team, as distinct from an issue.

key_definitions.plain_english: Risk that would help rather than harm. Managed the same way, and routinely forgotten.
key_definitions.apm_definition: Recognition that uncertainty can have a beneficial effect on the achievement of objectives. It is the positive side of risk, and it uses the same process and tools used for threats.

key_definitions.plain_english: Ranking risks by how likely and how bad. Enough for most projects.
key_definitions.apm_definition: Analysis that allows risk events to be prioritised, based as a minimum on the probability or likelihood of occurrence and the size of impact on schedule, cost, benefits and potentially other objectives.

key_definitions.plain_english: Putting numbers and probabilities on it. For large or complex projects, or to support an investment decision.
key_definitions.apm_definition: Analysis focusing on specific risk-based decisions, using techniques such as decision trees, sensitivity analysis, or a probabilistic approach such as Monte Carlo simulation.

key_definitions.plain_english: The live list of what might go wrong or right, what it would cost, and whose name is against it.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The record used to document risks, analysis and responses, assigning clear ownership of actions.

key_definitions.plain_english: Whoever is positioned to do something about it, not automatically the project manager.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The individual or group best placed to assess and manage a risk, assigned as each risk is identified.

key_definitions.plain_english: Acting before the risk materialises, to change its probability or impact.
key_definitions.apm_definition: A planned and implemented response, meaning 'we do something now'. For threats: avoid, reduce, transfer. For opportunities: exploit, enhance, share.

key_definitions.plain_english: Deciding in advance what you would do, then waiting to see whether you need to.
key_definitions.apm_definition: A response that is identified but implemented only if the risk materialises. A threat may be accepted with a contingent response; an opportunity may be rejected.

key_definitions.plain_english: How much risk the people funding this are willing to carry. Not the project manager's call.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The tolerance level for risk exposure, determined by the risk appetite of the investors and wider stakeholders.

body.where_this_fits: Risk is uncertainty that has not happened yet; an issue is uncertainty that has. That single distinction organises the whole LO and decides which process applies. It connects to LO19 (risks are identified during integrated planning), LO22 (contingency is the money side of the response), LO24 (issues and risk responses often become change requests) and LO2 (escalation exists because authority is delegated with limits). The most-missed idea: risk includes opportunity, and the same process handles both.

core_content.body_markdown:
## Change control: what it is
Change control is the governance around a project's baseline, plus the process and controls for spotting a change, weighing it and acting on it.

Why it exists: every project will change, and handling that badly produces plans that no longer agree, people who no longer know what is true, and consequences nobody intended. The point is not to prevent change. It is to prevent *uncontrolled* change.

And the purpose in one line: with a defined process, a sponsor knows what a requested change would actually do before deciding, which is what makes the decision a real one.

## Change control vs change management: the distinction to get right
| | Change control | Change management |
|---|---|---|
| What it is | The process governing changes to one project's baseline | A whole-organisation approach to transformation |
| Scope | This project's plan | The organisation and its people |

They share a word and nothing else.

## Change requests: where they come from
They arrive from all over:

- issues that surface while delivering, the LO23 link
- new stakeholder requirements, the LO16 link
- changes in the project's external environment, the PESTLE factors from LO4

The project manager is usually where a request first lands, and they then run the process.

## Change control: the six stages
| Stage | What happens | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Log change request | A change register or log records all requested changes | Nothing gets assessed informally, and rejected requests stay on record |
| 2. Initial evaluation | A first look at whether this even merits a full assessment. If it does not, it is rejected here | A cheap filter. Detailed evaluation is expensive, so not everything earns one |
| 3. Detailed evaluation | An impact assessment, covering how it may alter benefits, scope, quality, schedule and costs. It takes real analysis and input from a spread of stakeholders | This is where the real work is, and 24c covers it |
| 4. Decision | The sponsor gets the options, a recommendation, or both. Making sure a decision actually gets taken, whether approve, reject or defer, is the sponsor's accountability. The team is then told what was decided | Three outcomes, not two. And accountability sits with the sponsor |
| 5. Update plans | Plans are updated to reflect the change, and because the project's plans are integrated, that update has to carry through into scope definition, solutions development and configuration management too | 24e covers why this cannot be partial |
| 6. Implement | Necessary actions are taken, and the impacts are monitored through to completion | Approval is not implementation, and implementation is not the end |

Two stages carry more weight than a six-box diagram suggests.

Initial evaluation exists so that not every idea consumes an impact assessment. Rejecting at this gate is a proper outcome.

Monitoring after implementation is stage six's second half. The impact assessment was a forecast; monitoring checks whether it was right.

## The process: what it enables
Run this way, the sponsor and stakeholders can see what a change would do to the outcomes the project is forecasting. Specifically it should:

- keep decisions consistent with strategic objectives and with how much risk the organisation will carry
- handle the knock-on effects on other projects, programmes, portfolios and BAU

That second point is easy to miss: a change to this project can break another one's plan.

## Special cases: two situations worth knowing
A change implemented without formal approval. Run the process after the event. You do not pretend it did not happen; you run it through the process after the fact so the impact is understood and recorded.

And the framing to carry: this is not red tape for its own sake, it is the most reliable way to be sure everyone understands what the change actually did.

A change freeze. Sometimes a project stops considering change requests altogether for a period. Typically around exceptional points in its environment, such as Christmas or the summer holidays, so that avoidable risks and issues are not manufactured at the worst moment.

## Life cycle differences: where the stages vary
The syllabus asks about this specifically. Whatever approach or life cycle a project uses, it needs a defined process, but how that process operates differs.

| | Linear | Iterative |
|---|---|---|
| What is baselined | Scope is fixed at the deployment baseline, so any change identified in deployment must go through change control | Scope is held in a product backlog and fixed only for the current timebox |
| What counts as a change | Any variation from the approved scope | Changing what is already committed to the current iteration. New items simply enter the backlog |
| Frequency and ceremony | Less frequent, more formal | Frequent and lighter, because much of what would be a change request in linear is absorbed by re-prioritising the backlog |
| Where decisions are made | Sponsor and governance board, often at gates | The team may have authority to prioritise and act on new knowledge within the timebox |
| What flexes | Scope and quality drive, and cost and time are calculated from the scope | Time and cost are fixed, so scope and quality flex |
| Unfinished work | Becomes a variance requiring action | Anything the timebox did not deliver goes back into the backlog |

The structural reason: a linear project fixed its scope at approval, so every deviation is an exception. An iterative project only ever fixed the current timebox, so most change is normal operation. The formal change control process still exists in iterative work, and it applies to the things that were genuinely committed.

core_content.body_markdown:
## The change register: why the record matters
Every requested change goes into a change register, or log. All of them, including those rejected at initial evaluation. That record is what stops a rejected idea returning six months later as though it were new, and what lets anyone see how much change pressure the project is under.

## The change register: what gets captured
Drawing together what the process needs at each stage:

| Field | Why it is needed |
|---|---|
| Unique identifier | So the request can be tracked through the register to closure |
| Date raised and requester | Source matters, because a change from a regulator is not a change from a preference |
| Description of the change | What is being asked for |
| Reason or justification | Why it is being requested. Requests arise from issues discovered in delivery, new stakeholder requirements, or changes in the external environment |
| Priority or urgency | Whether it must be decided now or can wait |
| Initial evaluation outcome | Whether it is worth evaluating in detail, and the rejection reason if not |
| Impact assessment | The quantified effect on scope, objectives and success criteria, benefits, time, cost, resource, quality and risks |
| Options considered | Usually more than one, each carrying a different level of impact |
| Recommendation | What the project professional advises, and why |
| Decision | Approve, reject or defer, with the sponsor recorded as decision maker |
| Date of decision and communication | The decision is communicated to the project team |
| Implementation status | Tracked, with impacts monitored through to completion |

The test of a good change request: could someone who was not in the conversation evaluate it from the record alone? If they would have to go back to the requester to understand what is being asked or why, it is incomplete.

## Pre-assessment: three characteristics to check first
Before committing effort to a detailed assessment, determine the effort required by considering three characteristics of the requested change:

| Characteristic | The question |
|---|---|
| Size and scale | How large is it, and does it reach across the whole project or only part of the scope? |
| Complexity | Will this be technically hard, or is the solution straightforward? |
| Feasibility | Given what the project and the organisation can actually do, can this be done at all? |

These are worth capturing on the request itself, because they justify how much assessment effort was applied. And a change judged infeasible at this point can be rejected without further cost.
core_content.outcome_title: What a change request should capture

core_content.body_markdown:
## Impact assessment: what it is
An impact assessment is a structured way of working out what a change would mean for the baseline. It is what the detailed evaluation rests on, so that nothing the sponsor needs in order to decide properly is missing.

Speed matters, because quickly and effectively completing a detailed evaluation is crucial for success. A change held in assessment is a change the project is planning around without a decision.

## Impact assessment: the sequence
| Step | What happens |
|---|---|
| 1. Size the effort | Assess the change's size and scale, complexity and feasibility to determine how much assessment work is warranted |
| 2. Gather information | Draw on subject-matter experts and on data from inside and outside the organisation to pin down the specifics. The worked example being which technology best suits a software solution |
| 3. Assess work and effort | Nobody has designed the solution in detail yet, so the experts work to stated assumptions about how it would be built |
| 4. Quantify the impact | Against each area of the baseline |
| 5. Present options | Usually more than one, each with a different level of impact on the baseline |

Step 3 is worth noticing. You are assessing something not yet designed, so the assessment rests on assumptions, which should be recorded exactly as estimating assumptions are in LO19.

## Impact areas: the eight to assess
This is the directly examinable list, and each is phrased as a question:

| Area | The question |
|---|---|
| Scope | Does this fundamentally alter what the project is delivering? |
| Objectives and success criteria | Do the outcomes shift, or does what counts as success? |
| Benefits | Does it add new benefits, or disturb the ones already promised? |
| Time | Does the schedule move, out or in? |
| Cost | Does it push costs up, or take them out somewhere else? |
| Resource | Does this need people we do not have, or can the current profile absorb it? |
| Quality | Do the deliverables get better or worse? |
| Risks | Does it introduce risk, or retire some? |

Note how many are two-directional. Time can shorten. Cost can fall. Quality can improve. Risk can reduce. However, an assessment that only goes looking for damage will miss the case for approving the change, because a change is not automatically a degradation.

And note what the list covers: it is essentially the contents of the integrated PMP from LO19. That is the point. Put numbers on the impact, and look specifically at the rest of the integrated PMP when you do.

## Options: assessing them
Most requests get more than one option worked up, each landing differently on the baseline.

Ways to frame the options, drawing on the wider course:

| Option type | What it tests |
|---|---|
| Do nothing | Always an option (LO17). What happens if the change is not made? |
| Full implementation | The change as requested |
| Partial or minimum implementation | The smallest version delivering the essential benefit |
| Defer to a later phase or iteration | Same change, different timing |
| Alternative solution | A different way of achieving the same outcome |

Each is then assessed against the same eight areas, so the sponsor can compare like with like.

## Options: presenting them
Put real effort into presenting the options so the sponsor can follow them: summarised enough to be digestible, detailed enough that the decision is a sound one.

That balance is the skill. Too much detail and the decision stalls. Too little and the sponsor is deciding on a summary that hid the difficulty. It is the same principle as the integrated PMP in LO19, succinct enough to be used and complete enough to be trusted.
core_content.outcome_title: Assessing options and the impact of a proposed change

core_content.body_markdown:
## Change decisions: three outcomes, not two
Making sure a decision gets taken, whether that is approve, reject or defer, is the sponsor's accountability.

Defer is the one people forget. It is not indecision. It means the change may be right but this is the wrong moment: too close to a gate, inside a change freeze, or better handled in a later phase or iteration. Deferring keeps the request alive in the register rather than losing it.

Accountability sits with the sponsor for ensuring the decision is made. The project professional's job is the recommendation and the evidence behind it.

## Recommendations: what justifies them
| Basis | The argument |
|---|---|
| The impact assessment | The quantified effect across all eight areas. This is the evidence, and no recommendation is justified without it |
| Strategic alignment | Decisions should be made in line with the strategic objectives, which is the LO4 and LO9 link |
| Risk appetite | And in line with the appetite for risk, which is LO23 |
| Effect on the business case | Does the change strengthen or undermine the justification for the project continuing? |
| Effect on benefits | Would it create new benefits, or impact existing ones? |
| Impact beyond this project | What it does to other projects, programmes, portfolios or to BAU |
| Feasibility | Given what the project and the organisation can actually do, is this achievable? |
| Options comparison | Why this option rather than the others assessed |

## The argument: how to shape it
For approval: the change delivers benefit or avoids harm that justifies its cost in time, money, quality and risk; it aligns with strategy and sits within risk appetite; the project and organisation can actually do it; and it is better than the alternatives assessed, including doing nothing.

For rejection: the impact outweighs the benefit; it takes the project outside risk appetite or away from strategic objectives; it is not feasible with current capability; or the same outcome is available more cheaply another way. Rejection can also happen at initial evaluation, if the change is not worth evaluating in detail.

For deferral: the change is sound but the timing is wrong. A change freeze is in force, a gate is imminent, dependencies are unresolved, or the assessment itself is not yet complete enough to decide on.

## The decision: communicating it
Whatever was decided, the project team gets told. All three outcomes, not only the approvals. A team that never hears what happened to a rejected request stops raising them.

## Decision gates: the connection
Change decisions and gate decisions work the same way. A decision gate asks whether the business case is still viable, meaning whether benefits remain achievable for an acceptable level of cost and risk (LO6). A change decision asks the same question about a specific proposed variation.

And the governance board's own remit from LO2 includes reviewing and determining change requests, escalating them to a higher authority where necessary. So a change exceeding the sponsor's delegated authority goes up, exactly like any other decision beyond a limit.
core_content.outcome_title: Justifying a recommendation to approve, reject or defer

core_content.body_markdown:
## Partial updating: why it fails
Approve a change and the plans get rewritten to match it, and because a project's plans are integrated, that rewrite has to carry through into other processes too. APM names scope definition, solutions development and configuration management.

That phrase, *the integrated nature of projects*, is the whole argument for 24e. LO19 established that the constituent plans constrain each other, so moving one of them moves another whether you meant it to or not. Update the schedule but not the budget and you have two plans making different claims about the same project. That is precisely the misalignment, confusion and unwanted consequences change control exists to avoid.

## Updates: what has to change
| Plan or artefact | What changes |
|---|---|
| Scope definition | The PBS and WBS, and the in-scope and out-of-scope statement (LO17) |
| Solutions development | The specification of the chosen solution (LO17) |
| Schedule | Activities, durations and dependencies, and the critical path may move (LO20) |
| Budget and cash flow forecast | Cost baseline and drawdown profile (LO22) |
| Resource plan | New resources, or reallocation of the existing profile (LO21) |
| Risk register | Risks created or reduced by the change (LO23) |
| Quality plan | Acceptance criteria affected by altered deliverables (LO18) |
| Benefits | New or altered benefits, and the benefit profiles behind them (LO9) |
| Configuration | Approved changes reflected in the latest configuration version, with interrelationships between configuration items updated (LO16) |
| Business case | Where the impact is material, reapproval may be needed (LO4) |
| Deployment baseline | The amended baseline that delivery is now measured against (LO19) |

The configuration point is specific. An agreed change has to show up in the configuration itself: whatever it does to how the deliverables function or what they physically are gets written down and passed to everyone on the team.

Without that step, a change is approved and half the team keeps building to the old specification.

## Implementation: not the end
Then it gets implemented, and its impacts are watched right through to completion, with controls established to do that watching. The impact assessment was a forecast made on working assumptions about a solution that was not yet designed. Monitoring is how you find out whether it held.

Communicate it too. Approved changes must be communicated to stakeholders (LO17), and the decision is communicated to the project team (LO24a). A change nobody was told about is an uncontrolled change with paperwork.

## The updated baseline: why it matters
The updated plan becomes the starting point for progress monitoring. Everything downstream depends on it:

- Progress monitoring needs a baseline to measure against (LO20). Measuring against a superseded baseline produces variances that are artefacts of the paperwork rather than the work.
- Earned value compares actual and earned against planned value, which comes from the cost baseline (LO22).
- Change control itself assesses future requests against the baseline. An out-of-date baseline corrupts every subsequent impact assessment.

So failing to update plans does not leave one document stale and stop there. It degrades the control system that every remaining decision depends on.

## Unrecoverable change: what happens next
From LO20: when monitoring surfaces something the project cannot recover from, you replan and set an amended baseline. Change control is the ordinary route for a variation. Replanning is what happens when the accumulated position no longer works at all.

That is the honest closing note for the syllabus. Control does not mean the plan survives. It means the plan only ever moves for a reason, with the impact understood and someone accountable for the decision.
core_content.outcome_title: Updating plans and schedules to reflect approved changes

key_definitions.plain_english: The route by which a baseline is allowed to move: deliberately, with the impact understood.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The governance, process and controls that identify, evaluate and action changes to a project's baseline.

key_definitions.plain_english: A different discipline entirely. Change control is about the plan; change management is about the organisation.
key_definitions.apm_definition: A holistic approach to organisational transformation, distinct from change control, which is a process to manage changes to an individual project's baseline.

key_definitions.plain_english: Every request goes in, including the ones that get rejected. That record is what stops the same idea coming back unexamined.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The record used to log all requested changes.

key_definitions.plain_english: A cheap filter before an expensive assessment. Rejecting here is a legitimate outcome, not a shortcut.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The stage at which a change is reviewed to consider whether it is worth evaluating in detail. If not, it is rejected at this stage.

key_definitions.plain_english: The work of finding out what this change would actually do to scope, time, cost, quality, benefits, resource and risk.
key_definitions.apm_definition: A structured approach to assessing the implications of a change on the project's baseline, underpinning the detailed evaluation so the sponsor has the information needed for an informed decision.

key_definitions.plain_english: A deliberate window where the baseline is locked, around a go-live, a holiday period, a critical delivery.
key_definitions.apm_definition: A period in which no change requests are considered, usually implemented around exceptional events in the project's environment so as not to create unnecessary risks or issues.

key_definitions.plain_english: Not now. The change may be right but the timing is wrong, so it waits rather than being lost.
key_definitions.apm_definition: One of the three decisions available to the sponsor, alongside approve and reject.

key_definitions.plain_english: Where an approved change lands in the record of what is actually being built.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The technical and administrative activities that manage the creation, maintenance, controlled change and quality control of the project's technical configuration, ensuring approved changes are reflected in the latest configuration version.

body.where_this_fits: The last LO, and the one that protects every baseline the other twenty-three produced. Scope, schedule, budget, quality, requirements and configuration are all baselined somewhere in this course; change control is the single mechanism that lets any of them move deliberately rather than by drift. The distinction worth fixing immediately: change control manages changes to a project's baseline, while change management is organisational transformation. They are not the same discipline.
learning_outcomes: 24a) Understand the purpose and importance of each stage of a typical change control process (such as request, initial evaluation, detailed evaluation, recommendation, update plans and implement), and understand where these stages are different for linear and iterative life cycles.
24b) Know what should be captured and recorded in change requests.
24c) Know ways to assess options related to a proposed change and the high-level impact of the proposed change.
24d) Understand how to justify recommendations about whether to approve, reject or defer changes.
24e) Understand the importance of updating plans and schedules to reflect approved changes.

core_content.body_markdown:
## The business case: what it is for
Every project costs money, so anyone proposing one has to show that the cost, effort and benefit add up to good value for the organisation. The business case is where that argument gets made: options evaluated on time, cost, risks and benefit, then one recommended.

The sponsor is accountable for the business case. In practice, preparing it is usually delegated to project professionals working alongside subject-matter experts. That delegation is treated as good practice rather than a shortcut, because it brings the project team into the shaping of the initiative and builds shared understanding early.

## The five dimensions: questions every business case must survive
A business case has to survive five separate questions. Learn what each dimension asks, because a case can pass four of them and fail the fifth.

| Dimension | The question it answers |
|---|---|
| Strategic | Is there a compelling case for change, and does it align with the organisation's strategic objectives and other initiatives? |
| Economic | Does the return justify the investment: time, cost and resources set against organisational, societal and environmental benefits? |
| Commercial | How will it be paid for and how will resources be sourced? Is the deal achievable and attractive in the market? |
| Financial | Can the organisation afford it now, in the timescales proposed, or should it wait? |
| Management | How will the project be run in practice: team roles, governance, choice of life cycle, ways of working? |

The distinction people blur most often is economic versus financial. Economic asks *is it worth it*. Financial asks *can we pay for it now*. A project can be excellent value and still unaffordable this year.

## Business cases: storytelling documents
The strongest business cases put the technical investment appraisal alongside a narrative backed by evidence: how this team, working this way, is going to make it succeed. It is an unusual point for APM to make, and worth using, because it shows judgement and is examinable.

The reason is competitive. Most organisations have more problems and opportunities than funding, so decision makers are making trade-offs between viable initiatives. The case has to persuade, not merely calculate.

Without a clear business case, decision makers risk funding unsound work, leading to financial losses, reduced productivity, environmental harm and damaged stakeholder confidence.

## Creating a business case: the steps
1. Define the business need. Work with the sponsor to state the problem being solved or opportunity being exploited, and link it back to organisational strategy.
2. Analyse the options. With subject-matter experts, gather high-level estimates of the work and duration, resources and costs, the risks, and the societal, environmental and sustainability impacts.
3. Handle the uncertainty. The case is written early, when detail is thin. Counter that with proven estimating techniques, risk-based contingency planning and third-party assurance.
4. Agree a recommendation. Project professionals and sponsor review the options together and put one forward, showing how the work will be achieved: governance approach, chosen life cycle, how sustainability will be managed.
5. Seek approval. The sponsor submits it to a defined governance forum, an executive board or an investment committee. Approval formally starts the project.

Rigour scales to the life cycle. Linear projects tend towards detailed up-front analysis. Iterative approaches use a lighter business case, because the detail arrives as the project progresses. That ties straight back to LO1 and LO2.

## PESTLE, SWOT and VUCA: the three named techniques
The syllabus names PESTLE, SWOT and VUCA specifically. Each does a different job.

One line each, before the detail:

- PESTLE: what is going on *outside* that could affect this project?
- SWOT: what are we good and bad at, set against what the world is offering and threatening?
- VUCA: how predictable are conditions, and therefore how firmly can we plan?

These are general management techniques rather than APM-specific ones. The Body of Knowledge does not set them out as business case tools, so learn them as standard practice the syllabus expects you to know, not as APM doctrine you could quote back.

## PESTLE: scanning the external environment

Six categories of external pressure an organisation must respond to.

| Letter | Factor | Example impact on a business case |
|---|---|---|
| P | Political | Change of government policy alters funding or priority |
| E | Economic | Interest rates or inflation change cost and affordability |
| S | Societal | Shifting public expectations change what counts as an acceptable solution |
| T | Technological | A new technology reduces the benefit of the proposed option |
| L | Legal | New legislation makes an option non-compliant, or mandatory |
| E | Environmental | Emissions targets or environmental regulation reshape the options |

Use it to populate the strategic and economic cases, and to surface risks and assumptions early.

## SWOT: internal capability against external conditions

Four boxes on two axes: internal versus external, helpful versus harmful.

| | Helpful | Harmful |
|---|---|---|
| Internal | Strengths: capability, skills, assets the organisation already has | Weaknesses: gaps, constraints, things done badly |
| External | Opportunities: conditions the organisation could exploit | Threats: conditions that could damage it |

The axis pair is the thing to remember: strengths and weaknesses are yours, opportunities and threats belong to the world.

Use it to test whether the recommended option is one the organisation is equipped to deliver, which feeds the management case.

## VUCA: naming the conditions you are planning under

| Letter | Condition |
|---|---|
| V | Volatility |
| U | Uncertainty |
| C | Complexity |
| A | Ambiguity |

Coined by the US military to describe an increasingly vulnerable and unpredictable world. The key implication: inherent uncertainty makes it difficult to predict and plan with great accuracy.

The consequence for a business case is direct. Expecting full and perfect knowledge is unattainable in turbulent conditions, and forcing detailed planning and fixed-price contracting onto an uncertain future can be counterproductive and damaging. So under VUCA conditions the sensible responses are flexible plans, iterations, prototyping, options evaluation and scenario planning, plus a business case that expects to be revisited.

How the three fit together: PESTLE finds the external factors, SWOT weighs them against internal capability, VUCA tells you how much confidence to place in either. PESTLE and SWOT populate the case, and VUCA sets how firmly you are entitled to write it.

## Investment appraisal: how the economic case gets tested

Investment decisions are part of governance, so they need robust justification. Decision makers balance:

- Strategic alignment: do the outcomes fit organisational goals, policy, regulation and legislation?
- Affordability: is there enough money both to carry the risks and to land the benefits?
- Value delivered: will it return a decent financial figure, or other measurable value, across the economic life of the product?
- Portfolio effect: how does this sit among everything else the organisation is already doing?

| Measure type | Examples |
|---|---|
| Simple | Value ratio, net benefit, return on investment (ROI) |
| Time-adjusted | Internal rate of return (IRR), net present value (NPV) and its social variant NPSV, all three built on discounted cash flows (DCF) |
| Comparators | Weighted average cost of capital (WACC), organisational hurdle rates |

Time-adjusted measures exist for one reason: money now is worth more than money later.

Non-financial factors matter too: practicality, maturity of definition, and decision bias. Private organisations usually decide on financial grounds, while public and non-profit organisations weigh value for money, affordability and service.

One governance point worth carrying: independent review and scrutiny of the investment case should allow for several possible outcomes rather than one, particularly early in the life cycle, when uncertainty is at its highest.

core_content.body_markdown:
## A living document: why the business case cannot be a one-off
Projects run in complex environments where internal and external change happens daily. A case approved on day one describes conditions that no longer exist by month six. So the business case is maintained as a living document, continuing to show that the money is still being well spent.

## Undermining events: what can knock a business case off course
Five events come up again and again, and each one hits the case in a different place.

| Event | Effect on the case |
|---|---|
| New stakeholder requirements | Additional work and cost |
| Economic instability | Changes the cost and availability of resources |
| Technological advances | Reduce the benefit of the proposed solution, so the option chosen is no longer the best one |
| Organisational restructuring | Creates additional risk and uncertainty |
| Project team changes | Delays, additional cost, changes in approach |

The technological one is the least intuitive: the project can be running perfectly and the business case can still collapse, because something better appeared elsewhere.

## When to review it: use the control points you already have

A project professional cannot spend their time continuously re-examining the business case. Good practice is to reassess viability at governance and control points that already exist.

| Control point | What it tests |
|---|---|
| Change control | The impact of requested changes assessed against the project's baseline |
| Project reviews | Schedule, resources, scope and budget performance against forecast |
| Phase and stage-gate reviews | Whether the project is approved to proceed into the next phase |

That is an efficiency argument, and it is the reason 4b exists as a distinct sub-outcome. Continuous re-justification is not affordable. Piggy-backing the check onto existing decision points is.

## Significant change: what happens when it lands
1. The project professional brings it to the sponsor's attention. This is not a decision to take alone.
2. If the impact is significant, the sponsor may need to update the business case, or return to decision makers for renewed approval.
3. Decision makers decide whether the project should continue or not.

A project may be asked to pause even when its business case still delivers benefits, if other initiatives competing for the same resources are considered better value for money. Being worthwhile is not the same as being the best use of constrained resources.

## The business case as baseline: what that means
The syllabus asks you to know that the business case forms the baseline for the project. What that means in practice:

- It records the approved position: the expected time, cost, risks and benefits at the point of approval.
- Change control assesses proposed changes against that baseline, so the case is the reference point for whether a change is acceptable.
- Variance is measured against it. Reviews compare where the project actually is with what was approved.
- In extended life cycles it becomes the yardstick for benefits realisation, meaning whether the anticipated benefits appeared.

A useful precision, and one the exam distinguishes: the business case baselines why the project is worth doing and what it will return. The project management plan baselines how it will be delivered. Both are baselines, and they answer different questions.

## Lessons learned: feeding variances back
Where benefits over- or under-perform against the case, the variance is reviewed with the sponsor and the business case updated. Project professionals should then share lessons learned, so the next business case rests on better assumptions and sharper estimates.

Essentially, that closes a loop worth naming in an answer: business cases are written under uncertainty, so the only way they get more accurate as an organisational capability is by feeding real outcomes back into the next one.

worked_examples.ask: Delivery is perfect, so is the case safe?
worked_examples.answer: No. The benefit of your chosen option has dropped, so you take it to the sponsor. The case justifies continuing, not starting, and a flawless project can stop being the best use of the money.

worked_examples.situation: Month seven of a 12-month document rollout, zero variance on cost or schedule. A vendor releases a tool doing 80 per cent of it for a fifth of the licence fee.

misconceptions.right: It is live evidence of value for money, reassessed at change control, reviews and gates.
misconceptions.wrong: The business case is written once to get approval, then filed.

misconceptions.right: The sponsor is accountable. Preparing it is often delegated; accountability does not move.
misconceptions.wrong: The project manager owns the business case.

misconceptions.right: Economic asks if the return justifies investment. Financial asks if we can afford it now.
misconceptions.wrong: The economic case and the financial case are the same thing.

key_definitions.plain_english: The argument for spending the money: options weighed, one recommended, and the reasoning left visible so it can be re-tested later.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The justification for undertaking a particular project, programme or portfolio. It evaluates the time, cost, risks and benefit of different options before recommending the best solution to achieve the desired outcome.

key_definitions.plain_english: Five different questions a business case has to survive: is it worth doing, does it pay back, can we buy it, can we afford it now, and can we run it.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The five dimensions a well-rounded business case typically covers: strategic, economic, commercial, financial and management.

key_definitions.plain_english: Approval is not the end of it. The case has to keep being true, and gets rewritten when the facts move.
key_definitions.apm_definition: A business case maintained and updated throughout the life cycle to provide ongoing evidence that the project still delivers value for money, rather than a one-off approval artefact.

key_definitions.plain_english: The financial arithmetic behind the recommendation. Simple measures ignore timing; the sophisticated ones account for money being worth more today than later.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The evaluation of an investment decision using measures such as value ratio, net benefit and return on investment, or time-value measures including net present value, internal rate of return and discounted cash flow.

key_definitions.plain_english: The bar an investment has to clear before it is worth doing at all. Below it, the money is better used elsewhere.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The minimum target return an organisation defines for its investments.

key_definitions.plain_english: A checklist for scanning the outside world. Six headings so you notice the threat that is not in your industry's usual line of sight.
key_definitions.apm_definition: Political, economic, societal, technological, legal and environmental: the categories of external pressure an organisation must respond to.

key_definitions.plain_english: Two internal boxes, two external. What we are good and bad at, set against what the world is offering and threatening.
key_definitions.apm_definition: Strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats, an analysis pairing internal capability against external conditions.

key_definitions.plain_english: A label for conditions where confident forecasting is not available. Naming it stops you writing plans that assume knowledge you do not have.
key_definitions.apm_definition: Volatility, uncertainty, complexity and ambiguity, a term coined by the US military to describe conditions in an increasingly vulnerable and unpredictable world. Its key implication is that inherent uncertainty makes it difficult to predict and plan with great accuracy.

key_definitions.plain_english: The numbers may be wrong because someone wanted them to be, or because nobody noticed what they were assuming.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The risk that estimates are unfair, shaped by agendas or prejudices, or that psychological biases and blind spots are influencing decision-making.

key_definitions.plain_english: When the facts move far enough, the original approval no longer covers what the project has become. Someone has to say yes again.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The process by which a sponsor returns to decision makers for a renewed decision when changes significantly impact the timeframe, cost, risk or benefits of the initiative.

body.where_this_fits: The business case is the project's licence to exist, and the only document that can withdraw it. It links directly to LO2, where the sponsor is accountable for it and the governance board approves it, and it forwards into LO6 reviews, LO9 benefits and LO24 change control, all of which exist partly to test whether it still holds. The single most transferable idea in this LO is that the business case is a living document, not an approval artefact. Answers that treat it as something signed once and filed lose marks across several LOs, not only this one.
learning_outcomes: 4a) Knowledge of the tools and techniques used to determine factors which influence and impact a project's business case (including PESTLE, SWOT and VUCA).
4b) Understand the importance of regularly reviewing the impact of any changes in a project to the business case, and know that the business case forms the baseline for the project.
progress_checkpoint: I can define a business case as the justification for investment, evaluating time, cost, risks and benefit across options, and say who is accountable for it versus who prepares it.
I can name the five dimensions and give the question each one answers, and distinguish the economic case from the financial case.
I can describe how a business case is created, from defining the business need through options analysis to approval in a governance forum.
I can explain why the depth of a business case varies with the organisation's culture and the chosen life cycle.
I can expand PESTLE, SWOT and VUCA, explain what each is used for, and place internal versus external factors correctly in a SWOT.
I can name the main investment appraisal measures and explain why non-financial factors and decision bias also affect the decision.
I can give at least three events that can undermine a business case, and explain why a well-run project can still lose its justification.

I can explain why the case is reviewed at existing control points, what happens when a significant impact is found, and how the business case acts as a baseline distinct from the project management plan.
body.apm_learning_objective: Understand a business case as the justification for the initiation, investment and/or continuation of a project in terms of benefits, costs and risks.
